doNotEdit: Regenerate instead. This is a build product.

zones.purpose: The spot where pockets empty on the way in and refill on the way out.
zones.done: One tray holding keys and sunglasses, one wallet and one phone per adult, a single upright folder with fewer than ten sheets of paper standing in it, and bare surface on both sides of the tray.

steps.text: Empty the tray and the paper stack onto the floor. Keys that open nothing, loyalty cards, dead batteries and last month's flyers leave now. Every piece of mail gets a verdict of act, file, or recycle before anything goes back on the surface.

Put the tray where your hand actually opens on the way in, not where the furniture happens to be. Keys and sunglasses in the tray, one upright folder for act-on paper, and the charger plugged in at the far end away from anything that drips.
Lift the tray out and wipe under it, then wipe the tray itself. Keys shed grit and coins leave a grey film that tells you exactly how long it has been since anyone did this.

The charging cable and the umbrella drip line must not share a spot. Check what else is on the outlet feeding the dock, because a lamp, a seasonal heater and a four-port charger on one strip is this room's usual overload.

Photograph the cleared tray with the folder standing beside it, print it small, and tape it inside the coat cupboard door at the height people glance while hanging a coat. The tray then teaches itself.
When you sit down after dinner, the folder comes with you and you work it one sheet at a time until it stands loose and upright again.

zones.purpose: Hold the outerwear you will actually wear this week, at the moment you reach for it.
zones.done: One coat per person on the rail, one bag, hats and gloves together in a single labeled bin on the shelf above, umbrellas standing in the stand, and at least two hooks left empty.

steps.text: Take every coat down. Anything that did not go outdoors once through the last cold season leaves, and so do the single gloves you kept in case the other one turned up. Off-season coats go to a bedroom closet, not to the far end of the same rail.

Hooks for what goes on and off daily, hangers only for the wool coat that creases. Set the lowest hook at the height of the shortest person who uses it, and keep the two hooks nearest the door empty for visitors.
Brush the shoulders of the hanging coats, wipe the shelf where dust settles on top of the hat bin, and tip out the umbrella stand. There is always water and grit in the bottom of it.

Hang your full weight on each hook before you trust it with a soaked winter coat. Hooks driven into plasterboard without an anchor pull out later, with the coat still attached and a lump of wall behind it.
Write the contents and the season on the shelf bin, hats and gloves, winter, so whoever reaches up for it in October knows without opening the lid whether they have the right bin.
When you put a wash on, walk the rail on your way past and return anything that has been left over a chair back or the bannister.

zones.purpose: Hold the footwear that comes off at the door, and keep the grit it carried in off every other floor in the house.
zones.done: Two pairs per person on the rack, soles down, boots standing in the tray, one pair of slippers each, and a clear stretch of floor a full stride wide between the door and the rack.

steps.text: Pull every shoe out and pair them up on the floor. Odd shoes, outgrown children's pairs and the trainers with the split sole all go, and so does the tin of polish that has dried solid.

Daily pairs on the rack at a height you can reach standing up, boots in the tray because they will always come in wet, off-season pairs boxed in a closet. Nothing at all on the floor between the door and the rack.

Take the boot tray outside and hose it. The salt and grit sitting in it is precisely what scratches your hallway floor. Wipe down the rack shelves too, they hold more dried mud than they look like they do.

Wet soles on a hard floor are how people go down in this room. The tray has to catch the drip, and anything that walked in soaked stays on the tray until it is dry rather than being carried through the house.
Give each person their own named shelf on the rack, the name written at the shelf edge, so a third pair has visibly nowhere to stand and nobody has to count.
Shoes come off just inside the door and go onto the rack before the coat comes off, while your hands are still free.

zones.purpose: Somewhere to sit while you lace a boot, and somewhere to set a bag down for thirty seconds.
zones.done: Three items or fewer on the top, a seat with nothing on it at all, and a drawer where every divided section has one named category and you can see the base of the drawer between things.

steps.text: Tip the drawer out onto the bench. Dead batteries, pens that do not write, single earbuds, sunscreen from three summers ago and takeaway menus all go now. Anything you would not want while wearing your outdoor shoes belongs in a different room.
Divide the drawer into named sections and hold to them: dog lead and waste bags, sun cream and insect spray, a torch, one pen. Bags and the vacuum go underneath the bench, never on the seat.
Take the drawer fully out and tip the sand and crumbs out of its corners. Wipe the seat itself, which collects the same grit as the floor because people sit on it in outdoor clothes.

Fix the console to the wall if it is taller than it is deep, because children climb open drawer fronts like a ladder. Move the box cutter and the scissors out of the shallow drawer that opens at toddler head height.
Write the three permitted top items on a card and tape it inside the drawer, so the cap survives everyone who did not read this book.
When you clear the dinner table, carry the plates past the bench and take the top back down to three on the way through.

zones.purpose: Catch grit, water and road salt at the threshold so none of it reaches the rest of the floors.
zones.done: A coarse mat outside the door and an absorbent one inside, both lying dead flat with no curled corners, nothing whatsoever on the floor inside the door's swing, and a door that latches on the first push.

steps.text: Nothing is stored on this patch of floor, so the recycling bag, the parcel waiting to go back and the sports kit all move tonight. Give outgoing returns one named spot in another room and carry the rest to where they actually belong.

Two mats and only two. Coarse outside to scrape, absorbent inside to dry. The inside mat needs to be long enough that both feet land on it while walking, and most are not, which is exactly how the grit gets past.

Vacuum the inside mat on both faces, then take it outdoors, beat it and wash it. Run a cloth along the bottom edge of the door and along the threshold strip, because that dark line is all the grit the mat never caught.

A curled mat corner and a mat that slides on hard floor are the two ways this threshold puts somebody down. Grip or tape the edges flat, and dry the floor immediately when someone comes in soaked rather than leaving it to evaporate.
Run a thin line of tape around where the mat should sit, so a mat kicked out of position is obvious to anyone walking in rather than only to you.
The mat is on your route back to the cupboard with the vacuum, so it gets done last, every time, as part of putting the vacuum away.

zones.purpose: The stretch of counter where food is actually cut, mixed, and plated.
zones.done: One clear run of counter at least as wide as your largest cutting board, holding only the board, the knife block or strip, and the salt. The kettle and the toaster stand back against the wall with their cords coiled, and there is no mail, no fruit bowl, and no charging phone anywhere on the surface.

steps.text: Take everything off the counter and set it on the dining table, then let only three things back: what you cut on, what you cut with, and what you season with. The vitamins, the second cutting board, the bread bag and the pile of receipts find homes elsewhere or leave.

Put the board where you already stand without thinking, then build outward from it. Knives on a wall strip or in a block on your dominant side, oil and salt behind the board rather than beside it, mixing bowls in the cabinet directly underneath so you can reach one without turning around.

Lift the toaster and the kettle instead of wiping around them, because crumbs collect under the appliance feet and never move. Run a damp cloth along the seam where the counter meets the backsplash, and shake the toaster crumb tray out over the bin.

Knives belong in a block, on a magnetic strip, or in a bladed sleeve in a drawer, never loose among the utensils and never blade-up in the drying rack. Keep the kettle and toaster cords off the sink side of the counter, where a wet hand meets them.

Mark the clear run so it is not a matter of opinion. A short strip of tape under the counter lip, or the outline of the board itself, tells everyone in the house where the work surface starts and that it stays empty.
When you start the dishwasher, the board goes back down onto bare counter. If it will not sit flat, something has arrived that does not live here.

zones.purpose: The step of space either side of the burners where cooking happens with your hands busy and heat already on.
zones.done: Oil, salt, and pepper within one reach of the burners. A utensil crock holding no more than six tools, every one of which you used this month. Pot holders on a hook you can find without looking, the spices you reach for weekly at the front of the rack, and a clear landing space beside the hob wide enough to set down a hot pan.

steps.text: Empty the utensil crock into a box and cook for a week, returning to the crock only what your hand actually reaches for. The warped plastic turner, the corn holders, and the third pair of tongs are still in the box at the end of the week, which is your answer.

Arrange by the moment of need, not by shape. Oil, salt, and the turner within one reach of the burner, spices in a shallow drawer or tiered rack where you read the lids from above rather than shuffling jars, pans stored on the side you plate from.

Lift the burner grates off and soak them while you wash the splash wall and the underside of the hood with dish soap. Take the hood filter out and run it through hot soapy water, because a saturated filter stops pulling steam and starts dripping it back down.

Turn every pan handle inward so it cannot catch a sleeve or a small hand reaching up. Keep the tea towel, the paper roll, and the oil bottle off the burner side of the hob, and know where the fire blanket or extinguisher is before a pan is smoking. If the hob burns gas, three things belong in this pass. Know where the shutoff valve is before you need it, usually behind or beneath the appliance. Check that each burner actually lights rather than clicking unlit, because a burner left running unlit fills a room quietly. And if you ever smell gas, do not touch a light switch or anything electrical, open a window, leave, and call the emergency number on your supplier's bill from outside. Repairs and fittings are a licensed job, always.
Photograph the hob and one step of surround in its ready state and tape the photo inside the nearest cabinet door, so ready is a picture anyone can match rather than a standard only you hold.
While the pan heats, the spice you just used goes back to the front of the rack and any utensil on the counter goes back in the crock.

zones.purpose: The washing point for dishes, hands, and produce, and the place the whole kitchen resets from.
zones.done: An empty sink with a dry basin and a wiped drain flange. One brush and one sponge standing upright where they drain rather than lying in a puddle. The drying rack either empty or holding only what is still wet. Under the sink, a single tray holding dish soap, dishwasher tablets, and one all-purpose cleaner, with the pipes visible around them.

steps.text: Pull everything out from under the sink and line it up on the floor. Combine the three half-empty bottles of the same spray, bin what has separated or lost its label, and move out anything that is not dish, sink, or plumbing related, because that cabinet gets damp and is the wrong home for spare bulbs, paper goods, or vases.

Soap and brush live in a caddy you can lift with one wet hand, so wiping under them takes no planning. Dishwasher tablets go in a container beside the machine rather than across the room, and the towel gets a bar within reach of somebody already standing at the basin.

The sponge is the dirtiest object in the room: wring it out and stand it on edge after every wash, and retire it the day it smells while dry. Scrub the drain flange, wipe the rubber seal all the way around the dishwasher door, and pull the dishwasher filter out and rinse it, because a filter that has never come out since the machine was fitted is why the glasses come out gritty.

Never store bleach beside an ammonia or toilet cleaner under this sink, and never combine them in the basin; keep them apart, capped, and labels facing out. If small children live here or visit, this is the one kitchen cabinet that genuinely earns a latch.

Write the empty-sink standard on a card taped inside the cabinet door: dishes in the machine or washed, basin wiped, brush standing, towel hung. A standard is the best way you know today, written down.
The last thing before the kitchen light goes off, the sink gets emptied and the basin gets wiped dry.

zones.purpose: Light storage at eye level and above for the dishes you reach for every day.
zones.done: Everything used daily sits between shoulder and eye height, one category per stack, no plate stack more than about six high. Every mug can be lifted without moving another mug. The top shelf holds only what you need less than once a month, and the platter for eight lives up there.

steps.text: Count the mugs, then count the people who drink from them. The conference giveaway, the chipped one, and the one nobody ever chooses off the shelf come out first, because chips and crazed glaze are the easy calls and they shorten the argument about the rest.

Put dinner plates and everyday bowls at eye level on the side nearest the dishwasher or the table, glasses beside them, and send the serving platters and the punch bowl to the top shelf, where a step stool is an honest once-a-year cost.

Take each shelf completely empty before wiping, because the band of dust at the back is how you find out it has not been cleared in years. Wipe the underside of the cabinet nearest the hob, where a greasy film settles that you only see when you look at it from an angle.

Heavy and breakable do not belong above head height. The stack of casserole dishes or the cast iron lid stored overhead is the one that eventually comes down on somebody, so move that weight low. Use a real step stool, never a chair edge and never an open drawer front.
Label the shelf edge rather than the contents: plates, bowls, glasses, mugs. Then anyone emptying the dishwasher can put things away correctly without asking you where they go.
Emptying the dishwasher is the check. If a clean plate or mug has nowhere obvious to go, the shelf is over its limit and something on it is due to leave.

zones.purpose: Deep, low storage for the heavy pieces: pots, pans, lids, bakeware, and the big bowls.
zones.done: Every pan comes out and goes back in one motion. Pans nested no more than three deep or stood on edge in a divider, lids in a rack or on a door rail instead of loose, baking sheets standing on end, and the two pans you cook with nightly at the front of the cabinet nearest the hob. Nothing has to come out to reach anything else.

steps.text: Empty the entire cabinet onto the floor, which is the only way you will ever find the third saucepan and the wok bought for one weekend. Keep what actually cooked something in the past year. Nonstick worn through to the metal in the middle is not a spare, it is finished, and it goes to metal recycling rather than to the back of the shelf.

Nest by size but cap any stack at three, with a cloth or a sheet of paper between coated surfaces. Lids stand in a rack or on a rail inside the door, and baking sheets go on edge in a divider so you stop lifting three to reach the fourth.

Wipe the shelf floor itself, where oil creeps down from pan bases and holds dust into a tacky film that resists a dry cloth. While everything is out, twist every pan handle and tighten any rivet or screw that moves.

Keep the cast iron and the full stockpot on the cabinet floor, never above waist height, and lift them from a squat rather than bending over the open door. If a stack slides when the door is closed hard, it will one day land on a foot, so build the stack so it survives a slam.
Size the divider slots to your actual pans and write the pan on the front edge of each slot, so the wide skillet slot cannot quietly become the place lids get dropped.
When the pans are dry, they go back into their named slots. A pan that lives on the hob overnight is telling you its slot is too hard to reach, so fix the slot.

zones.purpose: The shallow drawers holding hand tools: flatware, spatulas, peelers, measuring spoons, foil and wraps.
zones.done: Each drawer has one job and a name written inside its front edge. Flatware sits in a divided insert with nothing loose beside it. Foil, cling film, and baking paper stand on end so you can read the boxes from above. Every drawer closes flush with one push.

steps.text: Tip one drawer at a time onto a tea towel and put back only what you have used since the season changed. Two can openers means one leaves. The takeaway chopsticks, the rubber bands, the unlabelled key, and the loose batteries are not cooking tools and do not go back in.

Dividers go in before anything else, and you name the drawer before you fill it. Flatware nearest the dishwasher, cooking tools nearest the hob, measuring spoons and the scale beside the baking cupboard, and wraps in the drawer you can pull open while holding a dish in your other hand.

Lift the insert right out and tip the grit, because the crumbs that jam a drawer collect underneath the divider and in the runner track. Wipe both runners and check that the drawer closes flush again before you refill it.

The peeler, the mandoline blade, and the loose paring knife are exactly what your fingers meet when you rummage without looking. Give every blade a sheath, a sleeve, or its own shallow tray at the front where you see it before you reach past it.
Write the name inside each drawer front: flatware, cooking tools, wraps and bags, utility. The name is the rule, and anything that does not match the name does not go in that drawer.
When you put the shopping away, the new roll of foil goes in on end, and anything that has migrated into the wrong drawer travels back to its own.

zones.purpose: Cold storage that has to keep food safe and show you what you already own before you shop.
zones.done: Raw meat sealed on the lowest shelf. Leftovers in clear containers at eye level, each with a name and a date on the lid. One bin marked for what must be eaten this week, sitting where the door opens straight onto it. The vents at the back wall clear of anything pressed against them, the door holding condiments only, and nothing in the freezer without a label.

steps.text: Work one shelf at a time so nothing sits out warming while you decide. Anything frozen past recognition and unlabelled goes, and every opened jar, sauce, and dressing gets judged against the date on its lid rather than by smell, because dressings and sauces go on smelling fine long after they should have gone.

Raw proteins go on the lowest shelf, where a leaking package cannot drip onto anything below it. Dairy goes inside the body of the fridge rather than in the door, where the temperature swings every time it opens. Produce goes in the drawers with the humidity slider actually set, and the eat-first bin goes at the front at eye level.

Pull the crisper drawers right out and wash them in the sink, because the sticky ring under a drawer is where a forgotten cucumber ended. Vacuum the condenser coils at the back or underneath, and wipe the door gasket in its folds, since a gasket usually fails from grime long before it fails from age.

Raw meat sealed and stored below ready-to-eat food is nearly the whole of cross contamination prevention in one move. Keep the rear vents clear so the compartment actually holds its temperature, and put a cheap thermometer on the middle shelf so you know what the fridge is running at instead of assuming.
A roll of tape and a marker live on top of the fridge, and nothing goes in without a name and a date on the lid. If it is not named and dated, it is not stored, it is abandoned.
Before you write the shopping list, the eat-first bin gets emptied of anything past, and the list gets written from the gaps that leaves.

zones.purpose: Holds the grains, pasta and cereals you actually cook from in a normal week.
zones.done: Every opened bag is either sealed in a container with its opening date written on it, or gone. Pasta, rice and oats stand as one block, breakfast cereal as another, and you can read the level in every container from the doorway without lifting a thing.

steps.text: Bring down every bag and box, open the ones already opened, and smell the flour and the oats. Stale, webbed, or bought for one recipe you cooked two summers ago means it leaves today.

Rice, pasta and oats go at chest height, in the arc your arm makes when you are already holding a pan. The specialty flours and the lentils you reach for once a month go on the shelf above, where standing on your toes is an honest signal about how often you use them.

Empty the shelf, vacuum the corners and the front lip where flour dust settles, then wipe with mild soap and dry fully before anything returns. Damp shelf plus grain dust is how a pantry starts to smell.

Fall, cut, or crush: cereal boxes and heavy grain containers stacked above shoulder height come down on somebody's head the moment the bottom one is pulled. Heavy containers low, light boxes high, nothing stacked more than two deep.

One container style for staples, one label per container carrying the item and the date you opened it, so a low level and an old date both read from three steps away. "A standard is the best way you know today, written down."

When you put the shopping away, the new bag of rice goes behind the open one and never in front of it. Loading in the wrong order is the single failure that makes everything else on this shelf pointless.

zones.purpose: Holds the cans and jars that turn an empty-fridge week into dinner.
zones.done: Cans sit in rows on risers with every label facing you: tomatoes together, beans together, soup together. No dented seams, no domed lids, no jar hidden behind another jar, and the oldest date in each row standing at the front of it.

steps.text: Take every can and jar out, turn each one until you find the date, and put the dented, rusted and bulging ones straight into the bin rather than back on the shelf. Then count duplicates, because four jars of the same pasta sauce is telling you exactly what you keep buying blind.

Rows by meal rather than by size. Tomatoes, coconut milk and stock together because they cook together, beans and tuna together because they are lunch, and tall jars behind short cans so nothing disappears.
Wipe the sticky rings where a honey jar or a sauce lid has wept, and wash the threads of the jars you open most. A sticky shelf edge is how ants find their way to you.

Poison, choke, or strangle: a can with a domed lid, a weeping seam, or a hiss as it opens is spoiled rather than merely old. It does not get tasted, decanted, or given to the dog. "Find it, and fix it now."

Label each row with its category and put the back row up on a riser so it sits above the front row. Once you can read every label without moving a can, the gap where the chopped tomatoes used to be is your shopping list writing itself.
When you sit down to write the shopping list, walk the can rows first and read the gaps. A missing tin of tomatoes is far easier to see on a shelf than to remember at a table.

zones.purpose: Holds everything you need to start a bake without a trip to the shop first.
zones.done: Flour, sugar and brown sugar in sealed containers you can open one-handed. Baking powder, bicarbonate of soda and yeast together in one small box with their dates showing. Cutters, cases and piping tips in a single lift-out bin, and no loose sprinkles rolling around the shelf.

steps.text: Test the leaveners rather than guessing: a spoon of baking powder into hot water should fizz hard, and yeast in warm sugared water should foam. The dead ones go, along with the brick of hardened brown sugar and the cocoa that has turned grey.

Build one lift-out bin holding flour, sugar, bicarb, vanilla and a scoop, so starting a bake is one trip to the shelf instead of six. Cutters and piping tips live in a second bin behind it, because they are the end of a bake and never the beginning.
Flour turns to paste under a damp cloth, so brush or vacuum the shelf dry first and wipe afterwards. Wash the scoop rather than burying it back in the flour between bakes.

Poison, choke, or strangle: almond meal, nut flours and sesame share this shelf with everything else, and one shared scoop carries traces straight into a birthday cake. Give each allergen its own sealed container and its own scoop, and stand it at the end of the row where nobody grabs it by mistake.

Write the opening date on the lid of every leavener the day you open it, because the printed date stops meaning much once air is in the tin. The bin sits in the same spot with the same contents, so a missing scoop or an absent vanilla shows before the butter is out.
When the oven timer goes and the bake comes out to cool, the bin goes back to its shelf with the scoop washed and the flour topped up.

zones.purpose: Holds what goes into a lunchbox, and what a child is allowed to take without asking.
zones.done: One open bin at child height holding only snacks you have already said yes to, and a higher shelf holding the ones that need an adult. Every reusable container has its own lid sitting on it, and the number of containers matches the number of lunches you genuinely pack.

steps.text: Match every lid to a container and bin the orphans in both directions, the lidless tubs and the lids for tubs that died. Then pull the snack boxes with two bars rattling in the bottom, combine them, and flatten the empty cartons.

Pre-approved snacks go into an open bin the child can reach without a stool. The ones that start an argument go on the shelf above their eye line. Lunch bags and ice packs stand next to the containers rather than in a drawer in another room.
Empty the bin and wipe it out, because crushed crackers and dried fruit-pouch drips collect in the bottom corners. Check every lunch bag for the sandwich nobody mentioned, and wash the liners.

Poison, choke, or strangle: whole nuts, hard sweets and grapes go straight from an open bin into a small mouth. Set the bin's contents by the youngest person in the house who can reach it, and think about a classmate's allergy before a nut bar goes into a shared lunch hall.
The bin is the rule made visible. What is in it is allowed, what is not in it needs asking, and a photo taped inside the pantry door shows what a properly stocked bin looks like.
When the lunchboxes come out in the evening, lids go back onto their containers and the bin gets topped up for the morning before anybody sits down.

zones.purpose: Holds the reserve that feeds the working shelves, and nothing else.
zones.done: Sacks of rice, cases of tinned tomatoes and packs of kitchen roll, each written on with the month it arrived, all standing at or below waist height. A maximum number written on the shelf edge for each line, and the count on the shelf sitting at or under it. Nothing stacked in front of anything else.

steps.text: Open up the back of this zone and meet what you forgot you owned: the second sack of rice, the twelve-pack of a sauce nobody liked, the case of sparkling water from a party in another season. Anything you hold more than one spare of moves forward into the working shelves this month or it leaves.

Weight decides height. Sacks and cases go on the floor or the bottom shelf on a board, kitchen roll and paper napkins go up top because they are light, and everything sits one row deep so you never move a case to see a case.

Sweep the floor of this zone and check the underside of the bottom case for damp, where a concrete floor or an outside wall is sweating. Cardboard that has gone soft is warning you about moisture before your food does.

Fall, cut, or crush: a stacked column of cases is stable right up until somebody pulls the second one from the bottom. Stack no higher than your chest, bend at the knees for the rice sack, and never store a heavy case overhead where getting it down means catching it.
Write a maximum for each line on the shelf edge, two of this, one of that, and mark every pack with its arrival month as it goes in. Undated bulk is where the saving quietly expires out of sight.
When a working container out in the pantry runs empty, you pull its replacement from the front of backstock and add the item to the list on the same trip. The gap on the shelf is the whole signal.

zones.purpose: Seat everyone for a shared meal without having to move anything first.
zones.done: One centerpiece on bare wood and nothing else, every chair pushed all the way in with nothing hanging off its back, placemats and trivets in the sideboard drawer one step away, and no paper anywhere on the surface.

steps.text: Clear the whole table onto the floor in one armful, then sort what came off by owner rather than by type. The homework, the unopened mail, and the half-finished craft project each go back to a person, not back to the table.

Placemats, trivets, and the napkin basket belong in the nearest sideboard drawer, one step from where you set the table. Anything you find yourself carrying in from the kitchen twice a day is sleeping in the wrong drawer.

Run a fingernail down the leaf seam and the joint where the top meets the pedestal, because that is where crumbs collect and stay. Wipe the chair rungs and the underside lip of the table where hands grip it to pull a chair in.

Lift and rock each chair to find a loose rung or a joint that has started working, and turn any chair that moves to face the wall so nobody sits on it before the joint is glued. Keep a trivet in the table's own drawer so a hot dish never lands on bare wood, and keep tall candles well clear of the runner ends.

The centerpiece is the table's only permanent resident and its footprint is the boundary. Photograph the table both set and cleared, and tape both pictures inside the sideboard door so the right state is not something anyone has to remember.
When the plates go to the sink after dinner, the homework, the mail, and the craft box ride along in the same trip. Nothing waits for a second journey.

zones.purpose: Hold serving dishes during a meal and a small, deliberate display between them.
zones.done: A taped run of bare wood at the end nearest the table long enough for the roasting pan, three display objects grouped at the lamp end, no paper on the wood, and the lamp cord the only cord in sight.

steps.text: Take everything off the wood, including the picture frames and the candlesticks, and give every piece of paper a verdict tonight: act on it, file it, or recycle it. Burnt-down candle stubs, dried flowers, and chargers belonging to other rooms leave now.

Keep the end nearest the table entirely bare for setting dishes down, and group whatever display you keep at the far end near the lamp. Serving spoons and the trivet stack live in the top drawer directly beneath that bare end.

Lift each object rather than dusting around it, then work the wax drips off with a plastic card and gentle warmth, and treat the pale rings left by cold glasses. Dust behind the frames and along the back edge where the wall meets the wood.

Trace the lamp cord from the shade to the outlet and count everything else sharing that plug, because a sideboard collects a lamp, a charger, and a warming tray on one socket hidden behind heavy furniture nobody pulls out. Move any candle sitting within arm's reach of a curtain or a wall hanging.
The taped run stays bare, always, and the display group is three objects at most. If you cannot set the roasting pan down without moving something first, the standard has already slipped.
Nothing sleeps on this wood overnight except the lamp and the three display pieces, so the last thing that comes off it each night is whatever arrived that day.

zones.purpose: Hold the things that only come out when the table is being set.
zones.done: Two tablecloths rolled with their matching napkins inside them in one drawer, serving bowls nested by size in the next, the large platters standing on edge behind a divider, taper candles of one length in a latched drawer, and a count card taped inside the door.

steps.text: Pull every tablecloth, runner, and napkin out and lay them across the table so you can see which sets are actually complete. Partial napkin sets, cloths with stains you have already tried and failed to lift, and serving pieces orphaned from sets you no longer own are finished.

Give linens one drawer and serving pieces another, and stand the big platters on edge behind a divider so you stop lifting three to reach the fourth. Roll each cloth with its matching napkins inside it so one pull brings out everything the table needs.

Wipe the shelves and the drawer runners while they are empty, then smell the linens, because a musty note means something went away damp and needs rewashing before it goes back. Check the silver-plate serving pieces for tarnish while you can see all of them at once.

Heavy stoneware platters and the punch bowl go on the lowest shelf and never above shoulder height, because they come down while your hands are already full. If taper candles and long matches live loose in a low drawer, move them to a latched drawer or a high shelf out of a child's reach.
Tape a count card inside the door: two cloths, one runner, eight napkins, four serving spoons. A ninth napkin arriving as a gift means an older one becomes a rag that same evening.
When a tablecloth comes out of the dryer, it goes back rolled with its napkins inside before it ever touches the back of a chair.

zones.purpose: Keep the good tableware safe, visible, and genuinely usable.
zones.done: Plates stacked no more than eight high with felt between them, cups standing single file rather than nested, glasses rim up on a clean liner, tureens on the bottom shelf, the cabinet strapped to a wall stud, and a photo of the finished shelves taped inside the door.

steps.text: Take every piece out and split it into three groups: complete sets, chipped or crazed pieces, and lone survivors of sets that are long gone. A chipped rim cannot be mended and is not safe to drink from, so that whole group leaves together.

Tureens and heavy serving pieces on the bottom shelf, plates and bowls at hand height, ceremonial pieces up top. Stack plates no more than eight high with felt or a paper plate between them, and stand cups single file instead of nesting them into each other.

Wash by hand in a plastic basin with a towel in the bottom, never the dishwasher for gilt rims or hand painting, and dry each piece straight away rather than leaving it to drain. Clean the cabinet glass inside and out and wipe the shelf liners while the shelves are bare.

Strap the cabinet to a wall stud, because a tall glass-fronted case loaded with plates is the heaviest tip-over risk in this room and its shelves are the right shape for a child to climb. Do not serve food or drink from decorative antique or hand-painted pieces of unknown origin, since older glazes can carry lead.

Photograph the finished shelves and tape the picture inside the door so the china goes back the same way after every holiday. When a shelf no longer matches its photo, something is missing or broken and you find out that day rather than next Christmas.
After any meal that used the good china, it is hand-washed, dried, and back behind the glass before anyone turns the kitchen light off.

zones.purpose: Make a drink and hand it over without crossing into the kitchen.
zones.done: Machine, grounds, mugs, then spoons and sugar running left to right along one liftable tray, mugs capped at the number of daily drinkers plus two, a marked fill line on the bean jar, and a hand's width of clear air behind the kettle.

steps.text: Line up every tea box, syrup bottle, and pod sleeve and check the dates, then open the travel mugs and match them to their lids. Anything past date, any mug missing its lid, and the promotional glassware you have never once poured into are out.

Set the station in the order your hands actually move: machine, then grounds or pods, then mugs, then spoons and sugar, then the way out toward the table. Leave a hand's width behind the kettle so its steam is not hitting the underside of a shelf.

Descale the machine on the interval its manual gives, lift the drip tray grate and wash underneath it where mould starts, and get the sticky ring from under the syrup bottle. Rinse the kettle and look at the element for scale while you are there.

Water and electricity share this counter, so give the machine and kettle their own outlet, keep cords back from the edge where a sleeve can hook them, and never refill a plugged-in machine over its own base. If wine or spirits live here, they belong behind a latch or high up, not on an open shelf at a child's eye level.

Mugs are capped at daily drinkers plus two, and the bean or pod jar carries a marked fill line that tells you when to buy more. Everything sits on one tray you can lift with one hand, so the counter underneath cleans in a single wipe.
While the morning coffee is brewing, you wipe the tray and top the jar back up to its line.

zones.purpose: Somewhere every person in the house can sit down without first moving something.
zones.done: Every seat on the sofa and every armchair is sittable without lifting a single thing off it. Throws folded to one size in one basket, at most one cushion per seat left in place, and both remotes in the tray on the arm with batteries that work.

steps.text: Pull everything off the seats and dig the seams out: the laundry that migrated here, the second and third throw blanket, the magazines wedged behind the armrest, the coins and hair ties down the back. Sort into leaves-the-room, goes-in-the-wash, and lives-here.

The remotes get one tray, and it goes on the arm people actually reach from while sitting, not the arm nearest the television. Throws get one basket at the end of the sofa, and reading matter gets one slot, so nothing has to be lifted off a cushion before someone sits.

Vacuum the seams and the deck under the cushions with the upholstery tool, then wipe the arms and the headrest where hands and hair oil land. Rotate and flip the cushions so the seat nobody chooses takes a turn at the wear.

Check the recliner footrest and the sofa bed hinge, and make it a rule that both close slowly with a look at the floor first, because that is where a child sits. Throws that trail off the sofa onto the floor are what people step on when they stand up in the dark, so the basket keeps them off the walkway.
Put the rule on the basket label itself: throws folded into the basket, nothing stored on a seat. "A standard is the best way you know today, written down."
The last person out of the room at night squares the cushions and drops the throws in the basket. It takes the length of turning the lamp off.

zones.purpose: A small shared surface for whatever is happening right now, and nothing that is not.
zones.done: One tray holding four coasters and the remote in use, plus at most one book or one plant beside it. No mugs, no charging cables, no post, and the wood or glass showing across most of the top.

steps.text: Clear the whole top onto the floor and put back only what somebody used in the last two days. The candle burned down to the foil, the coasters nobody uses because they sit on the far corner, the three-month-old magazines and the takeaway menus all go now.
The tray sets the table's entire standing inventory. Coasters go on it within arm's reach of whoever sits on the sofa, so a mug lands on a coaster without anyone leaning across the table.

Lift the tray and wipe the whole top including the ring marks, then get the underside edge and the lower shelf where crumbs and dust collect unseen. A glass top needs two passes, one for grease and one dry, or every fingerprint shows by lamplight.

A glass top or a hard square corner sits at exactly the height of a toddler's forehead, so corner guards or a different table is the real fix, not vigilance. A candle here is surrounded by throws, magazines and paper, which is the wrong neighbourhood for an open flame.
Photograph the finished tray and keep that picture as the reference for what clear means on this table. See Chapter 25, the ideal-state photo.
Whoever carries the last mug to the kitchen takes everything else that does not belong on the table with them, in the same trip.

zones.purpose: Keep the television, sound and consoles working, cool and cabled so a fault is findable.
zones.done: Every cable labelled at both ends, running in one bundle to a single labelled power strip. Nothing plugged in that serves a device you no longer own, a clear hand's gap of air around the amplifier and console vents, and every game controller and remote in one bin instead of four locations.

steps.text: Unplug and lay out every cable, then name the device each one serves. The composite leads, the disc player nobody has loaded in a year, the streaming stick from two televisions ago and the charger with the old connector all leave. Discs and games get one decision each: sell, lend, or recycle.

Bundle the cables by device path with velcro ties so one console can be pulled out without disturbing the sound bar. Controllers and remotes get one ventilated bin, set at the height of whoever plays, not on top of the unit where they slide behind it.

Vacuum the dust off the console and amplifier vents and the whole back panel of the television, because dust is what turns a warm device into a hot one. Wipe the screen with a dry microfiber cloth only, never a spray.

Heat and power are the two hazards behind this unit: keep the vents unblocked, never run one power strip into another, and look at every cable for a cracked or scorched section as you handle it. Anchor the television to the wall or to the unit, because a screen tipping off the front edge is the single worst thing this room can do to a child.
Label both ends of a cable the day it goes in and label the strip's outlets to match, so a cable that belongs to nothing is obvious at a glance. See Chapter 14, visual controls.
When you swap a device in or add one, it does not get switched on until its cable is labelled at both ends.

zones.purpose: Hold the books you will genuinely open again, and a small number of objects you actually want to look at.
zones.done: Each shelf has a hand's width of empty space at one end, books standing upright between bookends with nothing stacked flat on top of them, frames and objects gathered in two or three groups instead of spaced evenly along every shelf, and a strap running from the top of the unit into the wall.

steps.text: Take one shelf down at a time so every book passes through your hands. Duplicates, the manuals for appliances you replaced, the free paperbacks from a conference and anything water-damaged go now. Empty frames, the dead plant and the souvenirs you stopped seeing years ago go with them.

Group by how you actually hunt for a book, which for most people is subject first and author second, never colour. The heavy art and reference volumes go on the bottom shelves where a fall does no harm, and the hand's width of slack at the end of each shelf is where the next book lands.

Dust the top edges of the books themselves, not just the shelf boards, and wipe the shelf fronts where hands grab to pull a spine out. Do the very top of the tallest unit, which is where this room's dust actually settles and where nobody ever looks.

Strap the unit into the wall studs, because a tall bookcase loaded high will come over when a child uses the shelves as a ladder, and it lands loaded. Keep the stone and glass objects on the lowest shelves, and use a step, never the arm of the sofa, to reach the top.
Bookends plus a small labelled marker at the front of each group makes a misfiled book visible from the doorway, without pulling a single spine out.
When you finish a book, it goes back into its group that same evening instead of onto the coffee table.

zones.purpose: Put a light, a drink and one or two personal things within reach of the chair without turning the table into a nightstand.
zones.done: One small tray per table with no more than four items on it, a coaster under the glass, a bulb that lights and has been wiped, and the lamp cord clipped down the table leg so no cable crosses the floor to the chair.

steps.text: Empty the little dish and the drawer onto the seat of the chair. The reading glasses with the wrong prescription, the dried-out pens, the foreign coins, the loose tablets, the charger for a phone nobody in the house owns and the coasters that never made it back to the coffee table each get a verdict now.

One tray per table sets the limit, and it sits on the side the person in that chair reaches from without leaning. The phone charger gets a single clip at the table edge so the cable stays up on the table instead of hanging into the walkway.

Wipe the bulb and the inside of the shade while the lamp is off and cool, then the table top and the ring marks hiding under the tray. A dusty bulb throws noticeably less light, and light is the whole reason this table has a lamp on it.

Water and electricity meet here more than anywhere else in the room, so the glass goes on the opposite side of the tray from the lamp base and the charger. Loose tablets in an open dish sit at chair height, which is grab height for a toddler, and the lamp cord must never cross the path between the chair and the door.
Four items on the tray is the rule, and it holds because a fifth thing has nowhere to sit but the bare table top, where you can see it from the doorway.
When you plug your phone in for the night, whatever does not belong on the side table travels to its own room with you.

zones.purpose: Let anyone cross this room in the dark, carrying something, without touching anything.
zones.done: A continuous clear route from the doorway past the sofa to the other exit, wide enough for two people to pass and for the vacuum to run through without being lifted. Rug edges lying flat on a grippy pad, no cord crossing the route, and nothing on the floor but furniture legs, the rug, and baskets pushed back against the wall.

steps.text: Walk the route with a laundry basket and put every floor item in it: shoes, toys, yesterday's bag, the pile of post, the box that has sat beside the sofa for a month. Anything belonging to another room gets carried there before you let yourself sit down.

Floor baskets go against a wall or under the side table, never in the route, and each one gets a named category so it does not turn into a bin nobody empties. The route itself is permanently off limits for storage, including "just for tonight".

Vacuum the route, then move the sofa and chair legs and do underneath, because that is where pet hair and dust build up out of sight. Shake or vacuum the rug on both sides and press the gripper pad to check it is still tacky.

Curled rug corners, the lamp cord crossing the route and toys left in the dark are the three falls this room produces, and they happen at night to whoever is up first. Keep the route to the door clear at its full width in case you ever have to leave the house in a hurry. "Find it, and fix it now."
Full width, always, and you check it by walking the route with a full basket in both hands rather than by standing in the doorway looking at it.
When the vacuum comes out, anything still on the floor when you finish goes into the basket and gets returned before the vacuum is put away.

zones.purpose: Hold the television, consoles, and controllers so anyone in the house can start watching or playing without hunting for a remote.
zones.done: One console per shelf with its own controllers docked beside it, disc cases standing spine out in a single row, every cable labeled at both ends, the power strip off the carpet, and nothing resting on top of a vent slot.

steps.text: Pull every disc case, spare remote, headset, and loose cable out of the cabinet onto the floor. Anything that pairs with a console or a television you no longer own leaves today, and that usually includes two or three remotes you have been keeping in case.
Give each console its own shelf with the controllers and headset that belong to it, and stand disc cases upright in one row instead of stacking them flat where the bottom four become unreachable.

Brush the vent slots on each console and the back panel of the television with a vacuum brush head, wipe the controller grips and thumbstick collars with a barely damp cloth, and finish the screen with a dry microfiber cloth only.

Put your hand on the television and push gently. If it rocks, the anti-tip strap or the mount bolts need attention before you touch anything else in this room. Then move the power strip off the carpet and out of the line people walk between the sofa and the door.
While the cabinet is open, label both ends of every cable, and tape a small card inside the cabinet door listing which controller and which headset belong to which console.
When the credits roll, controllers go back on their dock and remotes go in the tray before the television goes off.

zones.purpose: Hold the toys that are in active rotation, at a height and in a form where a child can put them away without an adult.
zones.done: Five or six open bins with no lids on the lowest shelf, one category each, a photo of the contents taped to the front face where a child looking down sees it, the play mat rolled against the wall, and enough clear floor that two children can build without moving anything first.

steps.text: Tip every bin out onto the mat and make four piles: played with this month, broken, missing its other half, and outgrown. Anything with a cracked seam, a corroded battery compartment, or a missing wheel gets repaired today or leaves today, because it will not get repaired later.

One category per open bin, no lids, all on the lowest shelf: blocks, vehicles, dolls and figures, pretend food, art toys. A lid is one more step than a four-year-old will take at the end of a play session.

Wash hard plastic toys in mild soapy water and dry them fully, because a damp block goes back into a closed bin and stays damp. Fabric dolls and soft blocks go through the machine in a wash bag, and the play mat gets lifted so you can vacuum the crumbs underneath it.

For any child under three in the house, hold each small part against the middle of a toilet paper tube. If it passes through, that toy belongs in the older child's room, not in a bin at floor height in the shared room. Keep the tallest bin below the child's shoulder so nothing gets pulled down onto a face.

Photo labels on the bin fronts, and one printed picture of the finished shelf taped at child eye height on the wall beside it. Match the picture is an instruction a five-year-old can follow without an adult refereeing.
When the bedtime story is announced, the floor gets cleared first, and the story starts when the mat is empty.

zones.purpose: Store games and puzzles so that anything you pull off the shelf is complete and playable tonight.
zones.done: Boxes lying flat in stacks no more than five high, each with a strip of tape on the short edge naming the game so you can read it from the doorway, every loose piece bagged inside its own lid, and not one box on the shelf that failed its count.

steps.text: Open every box and count the pieces against the list printed on the rules sheet. Cards, tokens, and dice go into their own bags inside the box. A game you cannot finish counting is a game you cannot finish playing, and it leaves the shelf until it is settled.

Games lie flat and stack by height, heaviest at the bottom, tallest boxes on the lower shelf. Puzzles get their own short stack, because they are the ones that come down most often and go back least carefully.

Wipe the box lids and edges, which pick up a surprising film in a room where people eat. Check for soft or bowed corners on the bottom boxes, and shorten any stack that is crushing the box beneath it.

Dice, tokens, and the small metal pieces from older games are exactly toddler-mouth sized, and this floor is shared with the play mat. Keep game boxes above the reach of the youngest child in the house, and never park a heavy stack on the highest shelf where it comes down on a face.
Tape on the short edge with the name, plus a date written on the lid the last time the box passed a count. Anyone can see at a glance which boxes are verified and which are due.
On game night, the count happens as the box goes back, not as it comes out, so the next person is never the one who discovers the loss.

zones.purpose: Hold the throws and floor cushions people actually reach for while watching or reading, in a container that tells the truth about how many there are.
zones.done: One basket holding four throws folded to the same rectangle so the fold edges line up, two floor cushions stacked beside it, and nothing draped over the sofa back, the radiator, or the arm of a chair.

steps.text: Hold every throw up to the window light. Pilled through, thinned along the fold lines, or holding a smell that survives washing: those become car blankets, pet bedding, or rags, and they leave this room today.
One basket, and the rim is the limit. Fold every throw to the same rectangle so the stack squares up and anyone can see at a glance whether one has gone missing or one too many has crept in.
Wash everything in the basket, including the throws that look clean, because this is where pet hair and popcorn oil concentrate. Vacuum the basket's inside corners before the clean throws go back.

Look at where blankets end up when nobody is folding them. A throw laid over a radiator, across a floor heater, or hung on a lamp shade is the quiet fire risk in this room, and the basket rule exists partly to keep them off those surfaces.
The count is one throw per regular seat plus one spare. Write that number on a small label inside the basket rim, so whoever is folding can see the rule without being told it.
When the last lamp goes off for the night, whatever is on the sofa gets folded and dropped in the basket on the way past.

zones.purpose: Charge the household's phones, tablets, controllers, and headphones in one place, on a surface that can take the heat.
zones.done: One power strip on a hard surface, four or five labeled cables each ending at a named slot, the empty slots visible during the day, and no charger plugged into any other socket in the room.

steps.text: Lay every cable and plug out in a line and match each one to a device that is in this house and currently working. What is left unmatched is not spare, it is dead weight, and it goes to an electronics recycling point rather than back into the drawer.

One strip, one slot per device, the owner's name on the slot. Shorten each cable to the length that just reaches its slot, then clip the excess so the ends stay up on the surface instead of hanging toward the floor.

Wipe each cable end and check the last few centimetres near the plug, where the sheath cracks first. Blow or brush the lint out of the charging ports, because packed lint is why a plug stops seating properly long before the cable is actually broken.

Nothing charges on a cushion, a blanket, or a stack of paper. Lithium batteries need air, and a battery pack that is swollen, bulging at the seam, or too hot to hold is a stop now situation, not a weekend job. Put your hand on every device on the station once during this pass.

Name labels on the slots, not just on the cables, so an empty slot reads as a missing device rather than as free space. Keep the strip itself in view instead of pushed behind furniture, where a scorched socket or a chewed cable would go unnoticed.
When the dishwasher is started for the night, the devices come to the station and stay there until morning.

zones.purpose: Hold craft supplies grouped by activity so a project can start in one motion and the surface can be cleared for dinner just as fast.
zones.done: Four lidded, labeled bins (paper and card, drawing, glue and tape, kits in progress), scissors standing point down in a cup out of the youngest child's reach, one completely clear work surface, and exactly one project bin out on it.

steps.text: Test every marker on a scrap of paper, because the cap tells you nothing and the scrap tells you everything. Throw the dried glue sticks, the paint that has separated and will not stir back together, and any kit whose instruction sheet is gone and cannot be found online.

Pack the bins by what gets made, not by what the material is, so the drawing bin holds paper, pencils, and the sharpener together rather than sending a child to three shelves. One lidded bin lifts out and carries to the table in one hand, and goes back the same way.
Scrape dried glue and paint off the work surface with a plastic scraper before you wipe, get into the cracks where glitter sits, and stand the brushes bristle up so they dry without bending.

The glue gun is the real hazard here. It has no obvious off signal, its tip stays hot long after the last bead, and it gets left plugged in on a surface a child can reach. Give it a fixed cooling spot on a hard tile and unplug it before you clean up, not after. Keep the craft knife, the seed beads, and anything solvent based on a high shelf, not in a floor-level bin.
One project out at a time, and the label on the front of each lidded bin names what it makes rather than what it holds. That rule is what stops the work surface from filling.
When the table is being set for dinner, the open project bin closes and goes back on the shelf, whatever state the project is in.

zones.purpose: The bed and the linens on it have one job, which is to get you through the night without waking up.
zones.done: Bed made the same way every morning: fitted sheet, flat sheet or duvet, two sleeping pillows per person, one throw folded at the foot. Two complete sheet sets for this bed, one on it and one folded on the linen shelf. Under the bed holds either nothing or two labelled flat bins, and you can walk from either side of the bed to the door without stepping over anything.

steps.text: Strip the bed and pull out everything underneath it. Sheets worn thin at the hip, blankets gone pilled and scratchy, and pillows that stay folded in half when you bend them are finished; they leave as rags or textile recycling, not as spares for a guest who never comes.

Store each sheet set folded inside one of its own pillowcases so the flat sheet and the fitted sheet stop travelling separately, and keep this bed's linen on one shelf instead of stacked in with guest doubles and kid singles.
With the mattress bare, vacuum the whole surface and the seam where the protector tucks under, then run the vacuum head down behind the headboard where dust and hair pack against the wall.
Nothing goes under the bed that sticks out into the strip of floor you cross in the dark, and nothing heavy sits on a headboard shelf directly above where your head rests.

Write down what a made bed means in this house, down to how many pillows go on and whether the duvet is folded back or pulled flat, so it looks the same on the mornings you do it and the mornings someone else does. A standard is the best way you know today, written down.
Make the bed before you leave the room, while the duvet is still thrown back and it takes one pull. Come back at ten and you are moving yesterday's clothes off it first.

zones.purpose: This is your side, and it holds only what you reach for between getting into bed and falling asleep.
zones.done: On top: lamp, a lidded bottle or a coaster, one book, and a small dish holding your glasses. Five things or fewer, with no cable crossing the surface. The drawer has three divided sections with room left in each, and you can name what is in each one without opening it.

steps.text: Empty the drawer onto the bed. Dead pens, chargers for phones you no longer own, hotel earplugs still in their wrappers, and the four books you started and put down all go. A book you are not reading this week belongs on the shelf, not beside your head.

Divide the drawer so glasses, lip balm and earplugs each sit in their own section instead of sliding into one heap, and clip the lamp and clock cords down the back leg so nothing loops across the top.
Lift everything off, wipe the top including the ring the water glass has been leaving, then wash the lampshade and the bulb so your reading light is the brightness you actually paid for.
Water and a power strip do not share this surface. Move the strip off the nightstand top and onto the floor behind it, and if you drink in bed, drink from a bottle with a lid.

Five things or fewer on the top, countable from the doorway. When a sixth turns up it is almost always a finished book or an empty glass; the book goes to the shelf and the glass goes to the kitchen that night.
When you reach over to switch off the lamp, put the top back to five before your hand comes back. It takes seconds and you wake to a clear surface.

zones.purpose: This is the other sleeper's side, and it is the one zone in this room that is not yours to decide about.
zones.done: The top is clear enough to set a mug down without moving anything first, the lamp cord runs behind the leg rather than across the floor beside the bed, and any medication in the drawer is in date, capped, and closed away from a child or a dog who can climb onto this bed.

steps.text: You do not empty this drawer. Bring a bin liner and a box into the room, finish your own side first so there is something to look at, then ask whether they want the same. What they hand you goes. What they keep stays, and you say nothing about it.

Agree on the shared edge only: the floor beside this nightstand stays clear because you both walk past it, and the lamp cord runs down the leg for the same reason. What fills the drawer is entirely theirs.
Dust the top, wipe the lamp base and the switch, and vacuum the slot between the nightstand and the bed frame where tissues, hairbands and dust collect where neither of you looks.

Medication is the one exception to leaving this side alone. Check the dates together, screw the caps down properly, and if a child or a dog gets up onto this bed, move tablets out of the open drawer into a closed box.
Match the standard, not the contents. Both tops run the same item count and the same lidded drink rule, and what fills each drawer is each sleeper's own business.
When the sheets come off, both nightstand tops get cleared and wiped as part of the same job, so one side cannot quietly drift while the other holds.

zones.purpose: This is where your pockets land at the end of the day and where tomorrow's watch and rings wait for you.
zones.done: One valet tray holding keys, wallet, watch and rings, with nothing sitting outside it. Fragrance bottles grouped on a small dish, set back from the front edge. No folded laundry, no receipts, no loose coins on the wood. An anti-tip strap runs from the back of the dresser into the wall.

steps.text: Work through the pocket sediment: loose change into a jar that lives in another room, receipts binned or photographed, single earrings and snapped chains into one small bag you either take to a repair counter this month or let go. Jewellery you love but never put on moves to a box in the closet, not back onto this top.

One tray, and everything that comes out of your pockets at night lands inside it. Fragrance gets its own dish so the bottles stop wandering, and folded clothes never rest here on the way to the drawer.

Take the tray and the bottles off, wipe the top, and work at the sticky ring under the fragrance where the sprayer has been misting the wood for years. Wipe the drawer fronts and the handles while the top is bare.

A tall chest of drawers that is not strapped to the wall tips forward when a loaded drawer is open and a child leans on it. Fit an anti-tip strap into a stud, and keep the glass bottles back from the edge so they cannot be knocked onto a hard floor.

The tray is the edge. If the keys, wallet, watch and rings will not sit in it without stacking, thin the keyring or move a ring to the jewellery box rather than starting a second pile beside the tray.
When you empty your pockets at night, everything goes into the tray and nothing goes down beside it. That is the whole habit.

zones.purpose: These drawers hold the folded clothes you wear this season, split into categories you can find without digging.
zones.done: Each drawer holds one category: underwear and socks, sleepwear, t-shirts, workout clothes. Everything folded to stand upright so you read the whole drawer from above when it opens. A hand's width of free space in each drawer, and every drawer slides shut without you pressing anything down first.

steps.text: Tip one drawer at a time onto the bed. Out go socks whose partners never turned up, waistbands that have given up, the six workout tops you own when you wear two, and the t-shirts from events you no longer think about. Anything stained or holed becomes a rag or textile recycling rather than a donation somebody else has to bin.

Fold everything so it stands on its edge and the drawer reads like a row of files instead of a stack you excavate. Put dividers in for socks and underwear so the small things stop sliding under the folded rows, and move the heaviest categories, jeans and knitwear, into the bottom drawers.

Empty each drawer completely, vacuum the corners and the runners, wipe the base, and let it dry before anything goes back in. While it is out, check the runners and tighten any screw that has worked loose.
Open one drawer at a time. Two loaded drawers out together pulls the weight far enough forward to tip the whole chest, and a child using the open drawers as steps does it faster.
One category per drawer, and a hand's width of free space is the fill line. When a drawer needs pressing to close, that category has outgrown its drawer and one item comes out the same day.
When the clean laundry comes back to the bedroom, it gets folded upright and put into the drawer then, rather than living in a stack on the dresser top until the weekend.

zones.purpose: The closet holds the clothes you actually wear this season, visible and reachable in one look.
zones.done: One hanger style throughout, grouped by type and then by shade, every hook facing the same way. Shoes in pairs on a rack instead of a floor heap, bags standing upright on the shelf, belts on one hook. Two fingers of space between hanging items, a bare stretch of rod at one end, and floor you can stand on.

steps.text: Pull out anything you have not worn in a year, anything waiting on a repair you are never going to make, and every wire hanger and plastic sheath the dry cleaner sent home. Winter coats and heavy knits go into a labelled bin or the guest wardrobe so the rod carries only what this month asks for.

Switch to one hanger style so everything hangs at the same depth and the row reads flat, group by type and then by shade, and hang the short items together so the floor under them opens up for the shoe rack. Bags stand up on the shelf rather than nesting inside one another where you forget the inner three.

Clear the floor completely, vacuum it and the corners, wipe the shelf edges and the rod itself where hangers leave a grey line, and check the back wall and skirting for damp before the shoes go back down.

An overloaded rod pulls its brackets out of the plasterboard, and it does it while you are standing underneath reaching in. Lean your weight on it and see, anchor the brackets into a stud, and get the shoe pile off the floor so you are not standing on a heel in the dark.
The rod is full when you cannot slide two fingers between hangers. From there it is one in, one out, and the bare stretch of rod at the end stays bare, because that is where the next coat lands.

Turn every hanger backwards at the start of a season, and turn each one the right way round as you wear the item. When the season ends, the hangers still facing backwards have made the donation decisions for you.

zones.purpose: A bed a visitor can get into tonight without you touching anything first.
zones.done: Mattress protector on, one complete set made up on the bed, a second complete set folded inside its own pillowcase on the shelf, two pillows that spring back when you fold them in half, and nothing under the bed but one empty suitcase lying flat.

steps.text: Take every sheet set that has been demoted to this room and try each fitted sheet on the actual mattress. If a corner pops off while you are making the bed, it is a rag, not a spare. Fold each pillow in half and let go, and anything that stays folded goes out.

Nest each complete set inside one of its own pillowcases so a full change of bedding is a single grab from the shelf, and keep the spare set for this mattress size in this room rather than back in the family linen cupboard.
Vacuum the mattress surface and the seams with the upholstery tool, turn the mattress end to end, and wipe the top edge of the headboard, where dust settles unseen because nobody sits up in this bed.

Walk from the pillow to the door with the lights off, the way a guest will in the small hours in a room they do not know, and clear anything their shin will find. If the bed sits under a blind, tie the cord up out of reach of a visiting toddler.
Write on a tag tucked into each bundle: bed size, one fitted, one flat, two cases, one blanket. A standard is the best way you know today, written down.
Strip and wash the bed the day the guest leaves, not the day before the next one arrives, so the room sits ready rather than pending.

zones.purpose: The handful of things a guest needs in the middle of the night without knocking on your door.
zones.done: A lamp whose switch you can find by feel in the dark, one charging cable per common connector plugged in and reaching the pillow, a coaster, a box of tissues at least half full, and a drawer that is genuinely empty apart from a card with the wifi name and password.

steps.text: Open the drawer and take out what has been hiding in a room nobody uses: dead batteries, a clock radio that lost its time when the power blipped, three paperbacks nobody chose, cough drops fused into their tin. None of it belongs to a guest, and none of it belongs to you either.

Set the lamp on the side a right hand reaches first from the pillow, run the charger head over the top edge of the nightstand so it hangs where a hand lands, and stand the tissue box upright rather than laying it in the drawer.
Wipe the lamp base and the inner rim of the shade, vacuum the drawer out rather than wiping it, and clean the water ring the last guest left because they could not find the coaster.

The water glass, the lamp cord and the outlet all meet in one square foot here, so run the cord behind the nightstand rather than across the top, and keep the glass on the far side from the lamp. Take your own medication out of this drawer entirely, because a visiting child opens drawers before anything else.
Tape a small card inside the drawer with the wifi name and password, where the bathroom is, and which way the shower tap turns.
The night before a guest arrives, switch the lamp on and plug your own phone into each cable while you make the bed, so a dead bulb or a failed cable is found by you rather than by them.

zones.purpose: Somewhere a guest can unpack, so they stop living out of a half open suitcase on the floor.
zones.done: The top two drawers completely empty and lined, the lower drawers holding spare linens folded to one uniform footprint with a label on the inside front edge, an anti-tip strap fixed to the wall, and the dresser top carrying a lamp or a mirror and nothing else.

steps.text: This is where the household's undecided things hide behind a closed front: off-season jumpers, a bin of cables, wrapping paper and ribbon, a bag of outgrown baby clothes waiting on a decision about a second child. The jumpers go to your own wardrobe, the cables to the drawer that already holds cables, and the baby clothes get the decision today rather than another year of storage.
Put the empty drawers at the top, where a guest opens first and bends least, and the spare linens underneath, since you fetch those twice a year and they fetch socks twice a day.

Vacuum inside each drawer and wipe the runners, then leave the empty drawers open with the window cracked while you finish the rest of the room. Old wood holds a smell, and a guest's clothes take it on in one night.

A dresser with two empty top drawers is lighter at the top than it looks, and a visiting child will climb it. Strap it into a stud, and pull each drawer fully out to check that it stops rather than sliding free onto a foot.
Write on a label inside each empty drawer's front edge: reserved, guest. It stops the household reading a visibly empty drawer as an invitation.
During your own seasonal wardrobe change, you open these two drawers in the same trip and confirm they are still empty before the swap counts as done.

zones.purpose: Hanging space for someone else's clothes, plus whatever household storage this room has honestly agreed to carry.
zones.done: At least a forearm's width of clear rod with six matching empty hangers on it, a clear floor square big enough for an open suitcase, household bins on the shelf in labelled lidded boxes with nothing loose above head height, and a strip of tape on the rod marking where the guest section ends.

steps.text: Take everything out and put it on the bed. This closet is where the house keeps holiday decorations, a wedding dress in a zipped bag, a box of old phones, and paperwork from two addresses ago. Sort by whether a named person will use it in a named situation, and route the rest out.

Give the guest the end of the rod nearest the door and nearest the light, put the household bins at the far end, and use matching hangers throughout so the empty six read as an offer rather than as leftovers.
Wipe the rod with a damp cloth, because a rod nobody touches grows a fuzz that transfers straight onto a dark shoulder, then vacuum the floor corners where dust gathers undisturbed for months.

Anything stored above the rod sits over the head of whoever is reaching for a hanger. Move heavy boxes down to floor level and keep only light, lidded, labelled bins on the top shelf, with nothing stacked so the top item overhangs the edge.
Mark the guest boundary physically with a strip of tape on the rod or a hanger stop, so the line is visible from the doorway and does not depend on anyone remembering it.
Every time you take a seasonal bin down from this closet, you check the taped line and the empty hangers before you shut the door.

zones.purpose: Where a guest lands the suitcase, charges a laptop, and answers the email they came to this room to escape.
zones.done: A clear desk with a working lamp, a chair pulled up to it, a luggage rack or a taped floor square for the suitcase, one labelled bin holding a spare charger, wifi card, water glass, tissues and a folded spare blanket, and a reachable outlet with no cord crossing the floor.

steps.text: Clear the surface completely. It will be holding gift wrap, an ironing pile that never made it back, a printer that has not been switched on this year, and paperwork someone brought in here to deal with in peace. The ironing goes back to the wardrobe it came from, the printer either earns a desk somewhere it gets used or leaves the house, and the paperwork goes into the file it was always headed for.
Put the welcome bin where a guest sees it the moment they stand in the doorway, and set the luggage rack where a suitcase can open fully without hitting the bed frame or the closet door.
Wipe the desk and the chair seat and back, both of which collect a dust film in an unused room, and check the desk lamp works now rather than during a guest's first evening.

The classic hazard here is the extension lead run across the floor because the only outlet is behind the bed. Move the desk to the outlet rather than the outlet to the desk, and if a suitcase must live on a folding rack, open it and lean on it to be sure it holds a packed case without folding.
Photograph the room in its ready state and keep the print inside the lid of the welcome bin, so setting up is matching a picture rather than remembering a list.
When you carry the departing guest's sheets to the wash, the welcome bin comes with you and gets restocked on the way back.

zones.purpose: The place a child winds down and sleeps, and nothing else.
zones.done: Duvet pulled flat with one pillow squared at the head. Three or four stuffed animals on the bed, the rest sitting in an open basket at the foot where they can still be seen. Nightlight cord run behind the bed leg. A clear walkable path from the pillow to the door, wide enough to cross in the dark without looking down.

steps.text: Pull every stuffed animal out onto the floor and count what was actually in the bed. A child sleeps with a handful, not a herd, and the rest are drift from birthdays and fair prizes.

Give them bedding they can handle alone. One duvet in a washable cover beats a top sheet plus blanket plus quilt, because making the bed becomes a single pull instead of four layers a seven year old will never line up.
Strip the bed, vacuum the mattress, and get the strip of floor under it that nobody has seen since the frame went in. Wipe the headboard and the nightlight casing where hands land every night.

Blind and blackout cords hanging near a bed head are a strangle risk at exactly the wrong height. Cleat them high on the wall or change to a cordless blind. Then check the bed to door route, because a night trip to the bathroom should not end over a toy bin.

Tape one photo of the made bed inside the wardrobe door at the child's eye height. Match the picture is a standard a six year old can meet on their own, with no adult needed to rule on what made means.
The bed gets made while the school bag goes onto the shoulder, before anyone leaves the room. A duvet you can pull flat in one movement is the only version of this that survives a school morning.

zones.purpose: Holds the bedroom toys so a small child can put them away without asking anyone.
zones.done: Six open bins, none higher than the child's shoulder, each with a photo of its contents taped to the front face. Blocks in one, vehicles in one, small figures in one. Enough clear carpet to lie down on. One rotation box on the wardrobe top shelf, out of reach and dated.
