steps.text: Tip every bin onto the floor and sort into families first, blocks with blocks, figures with figures. Broken toys, orphan puzzle pieces and party bag plastic go out during the sort, never into a decide later pile that becomes a seventh bin.

One open bin per family and no lids anywhere. A lid is an extra step, and an extra step is the reason a five year old drops the dinosaur on the carpet instead. Heaviest bin on the bottom, the daily favourites at hand height.
Run the hard plastic through a sink of warm soapy water and dry it on a towel. Vacuum the skirting corners where small parts migrate, and check the bin bottoms for splits before you refill them.

Anything smaller than a toilet roll tube is a choking hazard for a younger sibling and belongs in a bin they cannot reach. Then check every battery hatch: button batteries are the serious one, so bin any toy whose battery cover has lost its screw.
Photo label on the front face of every bin, never on a lid, at the child's eye level rather than yours. A picture of six blocks works long before reading does.
Pickup happens when the bedtime story gets chosen, not after it. The story is the thing worth clearing the carpet for.

zones.purpose: One clear surface where homework actually gets started rather than avoided.
zones.done: Desk surface bare except a lamp, a pen cup and one tray holding live work. Laptop charger threaded through a clip on the desk edge so the plug never drops behind the desk. Books on the shelf above, none stacked on the surface. Chair empty.

steps.text: Paper first, and every sheet goes to exactly one of three places: live work into the tray, keepsake into the memory box, everything else into recycling. A worksheet from a finished term is recycling even when the marking was good.

Pens and pencils standing in a cup within a hand's reach of the writing hand, not across the desk where a reach knocks the water bottle over. Books and folders go up onto the shelf so the surface stays a work surface.
Clear the whole desk down to bare wood, wipe it, then get the pencil sharpener dust and dried glue out of the drawer runners. Wipe the lamp shade too, because a dusty lamp is a dimmer lamp.

Count the plugs under the desk. A lamp, a laptop charger and a strip plugged into another strip is where an overloaded socket hides, so bring it back to one strip in one wall socket. Scissors and craft knives point down in the cup, and blades go in a closed drawer if a younger child comes in here.

The tray is the standard: if it does not fit in the tray, it is not live work, and it goes to the shelf, the memory box or the recycling. Turn the tray out on the same evening the backpack gets emptied, so it never quietly becomes a second pile.
The desk gets cleared when the laptop lid closes at the end of homework, not the next morning. Closing the lid is the trigger.

zones.purpose: Holds the clothes that fit right now, at a height the child can dress themselves from.
zones.done: Rod lowered so the child reaches a hanger without a stool. Every hanger the same type, all facing the same way. Shirts together, dresses together, jackets together, with a hand's width gap between groups so a row can actually be read. Shoes in pairs on the floor rack, backpack on its own low hook, next size up in one labelled box on the top shelf.

steps.text: Pull anything that is the wrong size. Children's clothes fail in one direction only, too small, so the test is quick: sleeves above the wrist bone, waistbands that leave a mark, shoes where the toe is already touching. The next size up belongs in a box on the top shelf, never mixed into the rod.

Lower the rod. It is one bracket move, and it changes who is capable of using this closet. Then group by type and by colour inside each type, so getting dressed is picking from a row rather than digging through a jumble.
Empty the closet floor completely, vacuum it, and wipe the rod down where hangers have left a grey line. Check the top shelf for the dust that has been settling onto the stored clothes all year.

An overloaded rod on plastic end brackets comes down onto a child's head, so hang everything back on and give it one hard downward pull before you trust it. Heavy things, sports kit and boots and skates, live on the closet floor, never on the top shelf where a child pulls them down onto themselves.

One hanger style throughout, and the next size box labelled in numbers big enough to read from the doorway. At the start of each season turn every hanger backwards, so the ones still reversed by the end of it tell you what is not being worn.
The reversed hanger gets flipped forward as the garment goes back on the rod from the drying rack, so the record keeps itself and nobody has to remember anything.

zones.purpose: Folded everyday clothes a child can get themselves dressed from without asking.
zones.done: Five drawers, one category each, each with a picture label on the drawer front. Socks and underwear standing upright in rows so every pair is visible from above. Every drawer closes with one push, no pressing down. Dresser strapped to the wall, nothing on top of it worth climbing for.

steps.text: One drawer at a time, tipped out onto the bed. Out go the single socks with no pair, the underwear with dead elastic, and the pyjama bottoms that now stop above the ankle. Do not open the next drawer until this one is back in.

File fold upright so the drawer reads like a card index and the child sees every shirt without excavating. Dividers, or two shoebox lids, stop the rows falling sideways the first time the drawer gets yanked.
Pull the drawers right out of the carcass, vacuum the inside of the frame, and wipe the runners. That grit is where the drawer that sticks, and then gets slammed, comes from.

A chest of drawers with two drawers open is a climbing frame, and it tips forward onto the child climbing it. Strap it to a wall stud with an anti tip bracket. Then take the tablet or the toy off the dresser top, because anything a child wants up there is an invitation to climb for it.

A picture label on each drawer front showing what is inside, socks on the socks drawer, so the child both finds and returns without reading. Same category in the same drawer forever, even when that means one drawer stays half empty.
Refolding happens straight out of the laundry basket and into the drawer standing up, never stacked flat on the bed to be dealt with later.

zones.purpose: The square metre by the bedroom door where tomorrow morning gets assembled the night before.
zones.done: Backpack hanging on its hook at child height, packed and zipped. Shoes side by side directly underneath it. Signed forms in the front pocket rather than on the kitchen counter. Sports bag on the second hook, instrument case upright against the wall. Floor completely clear.

steps.text: Empty the backpack completely every Friday, turned upside down. Out comes the leftover lunch, the dead permission slip and the newsletter from three weeks ago. Sports kit goes into the wash basket, never back into the bag damp.

Hook, then shoes, then bag, along the wall in the order they get grabbed. The instrument case stands upright against the wall where it cannot be trodden on, and the lunchbox gets its own small hook, so an empty hook at bedtime tells you it is still in the bag with yesterday's sandwich in it.
Wipe the lunchbox seals and the inside of the water bottle lid, which is where the mould actually grows. Turn the backpack over a bin and shake it, then wipe the base where the drink leaked in March.

A bag left in a dark doorway at seven in the morning is the trip that starts the day badly, so everything hangs and nothing rests on the floor. Then check the things that must never be forgotten: an inhaler, an epipen or a dose of medication belongs in one named pocket that is checked at packing, not remembered at the school gate.

A five line checklist taped beside the hook at the child's eye level, in pictures for a younger one and words for an older one. Bag, shoes, lunch, form, kit. Five lines and no more, because a longer list gets skipped.
The launch zone gets packed while the bath is running, every school night, so it happens before anyone is tired enough to argue about it.

zones.purpose: The one surface in the house where your baby is left alone, which is why it holds a fitted sheet and nothing more.
zones.done: A bare mattress with one fitted sheet pulled tight to the corners, the sleep sack folded on the dresser, the monitor mounted on the wall with its cable clipped high and at least an arm's length back from the rails, and nothing draped over the top rail.

steps.text: Lift everything out of the crib and lay it on the floor where you can see it at once: the quilt, the plush pile, the bumper, the wedge, the stack of muslins. One fitted sheet goes back in. The plush goes to the toy basket, the muslins to the changing station, the quilt to the keepsake box.

Put the spares where your hand finds them in the dark. Two fitted sheets and one spare sleep sack in the top dresser drawer means a 3 a.m. sheet change is one drawer, one motion, and no ceiling light.

Strip and hot-wash the sheet, then wipe the mattress cover and every rail, especially the top rail where hands and gums end up. While the mattress is out, run your palm along each slat and put a spanner on the frame bolts; crib hardware works loose over months of being leaned on.

Drop the mattress to its lowest setting the day your baby can push up onto hands and knees, because the next thing they learn is pulling to stand. Move the crib clear of the blind cord, the lamp flex, and the monitor cable; any cord reachable from inside the rails is a strangling risk that comes down or gets shortened today. Find it, and fix it now.

Photograph the empty crib with its single sheet and tape the picture inside the closet door. Anyone who puts your baby down, including a visiting grandparent, can see what the crib is supposed to look like without asking you.
Every time the sheet comes off for the wash, the crib goes back together with a sheet and nothing else.

zones.purpose: A pad you can work at with one hand staying on your baby the entire time.
zones.done: Diapers, wipes, and cream all touchable without moving your feet or lifting your hand off your baby, a lined pail within one step, two spare outfits in the drawer directly beneath the pad, and a pad surface with nothing stacked on it.

steps.text: Clear the whole dresser top. What earns its way back is only what your hand touches during an actual change: diapers, wipes, cream, a burp cloth. The lamp, the framed scan photo, and the bottle of lotion nobody has opened all move off.

Stand at the pad and sweep your free arm through its full arc. Everything inside that arc is the station and everything outside it is storage. Diapers go on the side your dominant hand lands, wipes beside them, cream where your thumb can flip the cap without looking.

Wipe the pad after every change and pull its cover off for a hot wash weekly. Once a month take the drawer under the pad right out; that is where crusted cream lids and dried-out wipes collect underneath the spare outfits.

Keep one hand on your baby the whole time the strap is off, with no exception for reaching a shelf, because a roll off a dresser is a fall onto a hard floor from adult waist height. Anchor the dresser to the wall, and keep the wipe refill bags and the pail liner roll shut in a drawer rather than sitting on top where a hand can reach loose plastic.

Tape a card on the wall beside the pad with the counts you restock to: eight diapers in the caddy, one wipe pack open, one sealed behind it. The card tells you the station is running low before a bare baby does.
Restock the caddy back up to the numbers on the card during the last change before bed.

zones.purpose: Holds the sizes your baby fits this month and moves everything else out of the house fast.
zones.done: Each drawer holds one size only with the size written on the drawer front, sleepers and bodysuits filed upright so you read every collar from above, a next-size bin on the closet shelf, and an outgoing bag on the door hook with something already in it.

steps.text: Hold up each garment and read the size on the label rather than judging by eye, then check it against the size your baby is wearing today. Anything smaller leaves the drawer now, and there are exactly two destinations: the outgoing bag, or the keepsake box.

One size per drawer, largest size in the lowest drawer, and file sleepers upright on their spines so you can see the whole drawer at a glance instead of digging. Gifts in bigger sizes go straight into the next-size bin, never into a drawer you open half asleep.

Empty each drawer down to the base and wipe it out, because baby drawers collect sock lint and dried spit-up in the corners. Check hand-me-downs for stains that have set and wash them before they go in, not after you have pulled one out at 6 a.m. and found it.

Bolt the chest of drawers to the wall and never leave two drawers open at once, because an open drawer turns the chest into a ladder and a crush risk the moment your baby is climbing. Cut off decorative buttons, ribbon ties, and hood drawstrings from hand-me-down cardigans before they ever reach a drawer.
A written size label on the front of every drawer, changed the same day the size changes, so anyone dressing your baby picks the right drawer without opening three.
The moment a snap will not close over the diaper, that garment goes into the outgoing bag rather than the wash basket.

zones.purpose: Puts a clean assembled bottle or a full set of pump parts into your hands at 2 a.m. without a single decision.
zones.done: One bin of clean bottles assembled with teats and collars on, a second bin of used parts waiting, a drying rack standing empty, the formula scoop inside the tin with the lid shut, and a stack of burp cloths you can grab without looking.

steps.text: Line up every bottle, teat, valve, membrane, and pump part on the surface at once. Teats gone cloudy or split at the slit go in the bin rather than back in the drawer, and so does every part belonging to a pump or bottle brand you have stopped using.

Two bins in obviously different colors, one for clean and ready, one for used and waiting. Assemble bottles fully as they come out of the sterilizer, teat and collar on, so the middle of the night is a grab rather than a hunt for a matching collar.

Wash and sterilize on the schedule your kit calls for, then let parts air dry completely before they go into the clean bin, because a damp valve in a closed bin is where mold starts. Descale the kettle or sterilizer monthly and wipe the surface under the drying rack where drips collect.

Kettles, bottle warmers, and sterilizers sit at roughly the same height as the changing pad, so a pulled cord brings scalding water down at child height. Loop every cable short and run it behind the appliance, and keep the kettle and the water jug well clear of the socket and the monitor plug so nothing wet stands next to anything live.

Write the formula scoop-to-water numbers you actually use on a card taped above the station, so a grandparent or a night visitor mixes it right the first time. A standard is the best way you know today, written down.
When the kitchen light goes off for the night, the used bin goes down to be washed and the clean bin comes back stocked to four assembled bottles.

zones.purpose: Holds the reserve that feeds the changing station, in the sizes your baby is about to need rather than the ones on offer.
zones.done: One unopened pack of the current size and no more than two of the next size on a low shelf, each size written large in marker on the short end, a wipes carton with its count visible, creams and thermometer in one lidded box, and nothing at all stored on a shelf above the crib.

steps.text: Pull every pack off the shelf and read the printed size rather than trusting the picture on the front. Anything smaller than the size in use today comes off, including packs you have already opened, because a half-used pack of size 1 is still size 1.

Write the size in marker on the short end of every pack so it reads from the doorway, then shelve the current size at the front with the next size directly behind it. Creams, teething gel, and the thermometer go into one lidded box rather than loose between the cartons.

Wipe the shelf down and check the undersides of the cartons for damp, since packs stored against an outside wall wick moisture up through the cardboard. While the shelf is empty, read the dates on every cream and infant medicine and bin what has passed.

Nothing heavy goes on a shelf above or beside the crib, because a carton that works its way off lands exactly where your baby sleeps. Keep the outer plastic wrap and the pail liner roll out of reach, and keep diaper creams, teething gels, and any infant medicine in a closed box a standing toddler cannot open.
Write the minimum and maximum on the shelf edge itself: never fewer than one unopened pack of the current size, never more than two packs of any one size.
When the last diaper comes out of an open pack, the reserve pack moves forward to the front and the size goes onto the shopping list in the same motion.

zones.purpose: A short, calm set of things your baby can reach and choose without you handing anything over.
zones.done: Twelve board books standing cover out on a low ledge, one basket of soft toys filled level with the rim and no higher, the rest boxed in the closet as rotation stock, and a clear stretch of floor big enough for an adult to lie down on.

steps.text: Sit on the floor at your baby's eye level and pick up every book and toy in reach. Board books stay; paper-page books, torn spines, loose stitched eyes, and any battery flap that will not screw shut come out or go up on a high shelf until later.

Covers face out along the ledge, because a pre-reader chooses by picture and cannot read a spine. Fill the soft toy basket to its rim and treat the rim as the limit, with everything above it going into the rotation box in the closet.

Wipe the board book covers and the ledge, since chewed corners and drool are essentially the whole cleaning job in this zone. Run soft toys through a monthly wash and check tags, seams, and stitched eyes as you pull each one out of the machine.

Bolt the shelf or ledge to the wall, because the day your baby pulls to standing it becomes the nearest handhold and a tip-over risk. Check every light-up or musical toy for a battery compartment that needs a screwdriver, and remove anything with a loose button battery or a ribbon tag long enough to wind around a wrist.
Twelve covers on the ledge, one basket level with its rim. Anything new that arrives means something goes into the rotation box the same day, not the same month.
When you switch the lamp off after the bedtime story, stand the books back cover out and swap two off the ledge for two out of the rotation box.

zones.purpose: To hold the handful of things you touch every morning and every night, and nothing else.
zones.done: One tray you can lift with one hand, holding soap, the toothbrush holder, and no more than four daily products. Bare stone on both sides of the basin, a mirror with no splatter, and no cord crossing the sink.

steps.text: Pull everything off the counter onto a towel and put back only what your hands touched today and yesterday. The travel bottles, the sample sachets, and the hair tie graveyard go into a drawer or out of the room entirely.
Give the daily set one tray, on the side you reach with your dominant hand. The heat tool gets a heat-safe rest and its cord parks behind the basin rather than draped across it.
Wipe the tray, then the counter under it, then the base of the faucet where toothpaste dries into a crust. Finish with the mirror and the light switch plate, the thing in this room nobody ever wipes.

Water and a plugged-in dryer share one small surface in here. Keep the cord on the far side of the basin from the tap, and pull the plug at the wall the moment you set the tool down, not once your hair is finished.
Write the four-product limit on a strip of tape stuck under the tray, and tape a photo of the cleared counter inside the vanity door. A fifth bottle then has something to argue with before it lands.
When you rinse your toothbrush at night, the tray goes back to match the photo before the light goes off. Same moment, every night.

zones.purpose: To hold the grooming tools and products you actually reach for, arranged by when in the day you use them.
zones.done: Every drawer divided, nothing past its open-jar window, razor blades capped or in a lidded box in one corner, and a top drawer you can read in a single look without moving anything.

steps.text: Empty one drawer at a time onto a towel and turn every tube, jar, and bottle over to find a date or an open-jar symbol. Mascara, liquid foundation, and sunscreen are the usual offenders; dead hair ties and orphan bobby pins are the usual volume.

Divide by routine rather than by product type: a morning compartment, an evening compartment, and one for weekly and occasional. Combs, brushes, and dental supplies stand upright in their own section so nothing has to be dug through.

Lift the dividers out and tip the drawer over a bin, because loose powder, hair, and grit collect underneath where you never look. Wipe the drawer bottom and the runners, then wipe the dividers before they go back in.
Loose blades and razor cartridges in a drawer you reach into blind will find a fingertip. Cap every blade, or give all razors one lidded box in a fixed corner you never grope past.
Write a count on each divider label: two lipsticks in rotation, one comb, one brush. A third lipstick has to beat one of the two already in the slot before it gets to stay.
On laundry day, while you are already carrying towels into the room, pull the top drawer and lift out anything empty or dried out. One drawer, one look, a week of drift undone.

zones.purpose: To store cleaning supplies and backstock around the plumbing without ever hiding a leak.
zones.done: Two pull-out bins clear of the P-trap, a pale tray on the cabinet floor with nothing stacked on it, one open bottle per job, and both shut-off valves in plain sight when the doors swing open.

steps.text: Take it all out and line it up on the floor by job: glass, tub and tile, toilet, drain, polish. You will find three half-full bottles of the same thing and one you cannot identify, and the one you cannot identify goes.

Build the bins around the P-trap instead of fighting it, keeping the joint and the valves visible. Paper goods and bulk toiletries take the side with headroom, and sprays sit at the front where you can read a label without kneeling.

Wipe the cabinet floor and look hard for a dark ring or a soft patch in the board, which is what a slow leak looks like before it looks like water. Wipe the neck of every bottle before it goes back so the pale tray never turns sticky.

Never store bleach where it can tip into an ammonia-based cleaner, and never decant anything into a drink bottle. This cabinet sits at toddler height, so if small children come through the house, fit a magnetic catch or move the chemistry above the sink line.
One open container per job, backstock capped at two. Label the front edge of each bin with the job rather than the brand, so the bowl cleaner cannot quietly end up among the glass sprays.
When you refill the hand soap at the basin, crouch and run your eyes over the cabinet floor and the trap joint before you close the doors. That is the entire leak check.

zones.purpose: To hold the medicine and first aid you would need tonight, and nothing you stopped needing years ago.
zones.done: Three labeled bins, pain relief, stomach and cold, first aid, each holding only in-date items. Prescriptions grouped by the name on the label, the first aid bin small enough to carry one-handed to whoever is bleeding, and the whole cabinet above a child's reach with a catch on it if children are in the house.

steps.text: Read every label and every date, including the small print on the boxes you kept because the box was still good. Anything expired, anything unlabeled, and anything prescribed for a condition nobody here has now goes straight into a bag for the pharmacy take-back.
Group by the reason you come to this cabinet: headache, stomach, cut, cold, eyes. Put the two things you reach for at two in the morning on the shelf you can find without turning the light on.

Take the shelves out and wash off the sticky rings left by cough syrup and the dust of old blister foil. Dry them all the way through before they go back, because a damp shelf is what turns tablets chalky in here.

Bathroom humidity breaks tablets and capsules down faster than a bedroom shelf does, so move anything you take daily out of this room entirely. Whatever stays gets a child-secure catch, and nothing ever goes down the toilet.

Bins are labeled by symptom rather than brand, so a guest or a sitter can find what they need without asking which box the cold tablets are in. The first aid bin holds plasters, tape, gauze, and one pair of scissors, and it never becomes a home for spare vitamins.

Every time you come home from the pharmacy, the new box goes into its bin and you read the dates of everything already in that bin before you shut the door. The take-back bag then rides back with you on the next trip.

zones.purpose: To keep only the products actually in use within reach, on surfaces that dry out between showers.
zones.done: One shampoo, one conditioner, one wash, and one bar per person in the caddy. A squeegee on its hook inside the enclosure, grip strips or a mat with real suction on the floor, and no dark line where the wall meets the tray.

steps.text: Line every bottle along the tub edge and shake each one. The ones you cannot remember using this month, the conditioner that did nothing, and the hotel bottles all leave, and the nearly-empty ones get finished this week or poured together.

Give each person their own shelf or corner of the caddy instead of one mixed crowd, and hang the squeegee where a wet hand meets it without leaning out over the tub wall. Bottles go cap-down only if they truly seal, otherwise they ring the shelf.

Spray the walls and the tray, then step out and do the counter or the toilet while the cleaner works. Come back, wipe, rinse, squeegee glass and tile from the top down, and leave the door standing open.

Wet glaze under a film of soap is the most slippery surface in the house, so the mat or the grip strips are not optional, and a grab bar is a morning's work to fit. Razors go on a high hook, never on the tub edge where a small hand reaches for balance.
Hold the caddy to a bottle limit: a new bottle comes in only on the day an empty goes out. The squeegee has one hook and hangs on it wet, every time.
Last person out squeegees the glass and the walls, props the door open, and leaves the fan running. It happens while you are already wet and standing there.

zones.purpose: To keep the smallest and dirtiest patch of the room clean and stocked without letting it contaminate anything else.
zones.done: Two reserve rolls within reach from a seated position and the rest of the pack in the cupboard. The brush in a holder that has been emptied and dried, a lined bin with a lid, and a completely bare cistern lid.

steps.text: Clear the cistern top down to the porcelain: the candle, the spare hand cream, the phone charger, the stack of reading. Everything stored up there has been sitting inside the fine spray a flush throws, and most of it does not belong in this room at all.

Two reserve rolls go in a holder you can reach sitting down, and the rest of the pack goes to the linen cupboard. The brush and the bin each get a marked spot on the floor so a mop has a clean run around the pedestal.

Treat the bowl and let it sit while you do the rest of the room, then work the outside in order: handle, lid, seat top, seat underside, rim, pedestal, and the floor around the base where drips land. One cloth, one color, this job only.

Bowl cleaner is the harshest chemistry in the house and must never meet bleach in the same bowl. Store it high or in the under-sink cabinet behind a catch, not on the floor beside the pedestal where a child stands to reach the flush.
The toilet cloth and the toilet gloves are a color no other job in the house uses, and they hang apart from every other cloth. Two reserve rolls is the floor; dropping to one is the restock signal.
Whoever hangs the last roll carries two more in from the cupboard on their next trip through. The empty holder does the remembering, not you.

zones.purpose: To hold enough clean towels for the way this house actually does laundry, and no more than the shelf can safely carry.
zones.done: Three bath towels per person, one in use, one in the wash, one folded on the shelf. Each guest set nested in its own pillowcase, hand towels and washcloths in separate labeled columns, and a spare bath mat rolled at the end of the shelf.

steps.text: Take every towel out and rank them by which one your hand actually goes to after a shower. The thin, the stiff, the shedders, and the odd single from a lost set all leave, with the best of the rejects becoming cleaning rags and the rest going to a shelter that takes textiles.

Fold everything to one width so the stack squares up, then keep bath towels, hand towels, and washcloths in their own columns rather than one mixed pile. Each guest set goes inside a pillowcase so the whole set lifts off the shelf in one grab.

Wipe the shelves and press the back wall for damp, because a towel put away not quite dry will scent the whole cupboard within days. Anything sour goes back through a hot wash with no softener before it returns.

A deep stack of linens on a shelf held by four small brackets is a load nobody ever weighed. Check the brackets and the wall fixings, and keep the heavy bath towels on the lower shelves so nothing tall comes down on your head.

The count is the standard: three bath towels per person, folded to one width, one label per column. When a column is full and clean laundry arrives, the most worn towel in that column becomes a rag that day.

When you fold laundry, clean towels go to the bottom of their column so the oldest keeps coming to your hand, and you check the column count in the same motion. Nothing goes onto the shelf damp, ever.

zones.purpose: It gives a visitor somewhere to wash their hands and set a phone down, with nothing of yours in the way.
zones.done: A soap pump above half full, one folded hand towel on the ring where you can see it from the doorway, a box of tissues at the back corner, and enough bare counter to set down a phone and a pair of glasses. No toothbrush cup holding your family's toothbrushes, no hair clips behind the tap, no dried soap ring under the dispenser.

steps.text: Take everything off the counter and put back only what a visitor would use: soap, tissues, hand towel. The travel conditioner, the spare contact lens case, and the razor that ended up here because the main bathroom ran out of room all go back where they belong or into the trash.

Set the soap on the side your hand reaches without crossing over the basin, tissues at the back corner clear of splash, and the hand towel on a ring or hook visible from the door. A guest should never have to open a cabinet to find a towel.

Wipe the counter, then the tap and the drain lip where toothpaste film and hard water scale build up, including the collar at the base of the tap where a chalky ring hides. Do the mirror last, top to bottom, so drips land on surfaces you have not finished yet.

Water and electricity: a shaver or hair dryer left plugged in beside a full basin is a live cord within splash reach, so unplug it and put it away rather than coiling it on the counter. Swap any glass tumbler or glass trinket dish for ceramic, because glass on a wet counter slides and it breaks onto a tile floor where feet are bare.

Three things live on this counter permanently: soap, tissues, hand towel. Photograph that exact arrangement and tape the picture inside the vanity door, so anyone in the house can reset the counter without asking you which three.

The moment someone confirms they are coming over, walk in, top up the soap, and hang a fresh hand towel. Soap level and towel are the two things a visitor registers, and both are handled before you have put the phone down.

zones.purpose: It holds the things a guest might otherwise have to ask you for, plus the cleaning kit that keeps this room ready.
zones.done: Open the door and see two lift-out bins and nothing loose: one labeled for guest supplies holding a new toothbrush, a wrapped bar of soap, and four unopened travel toiletries in a small dish, and one labeled for cleaning holding bowl cleaner, glass spray, and cloths standing upright on a shallow tray. Four rolls of toilet paper stacked in plain view. The cabinet base is bare enough that a single drip from the trap would show.

steps.text: Pull everything out and be honest about the hotel miniatures: the shampoos from three trips, the lotion nobody opened, the free conditioner samples. Keep the unopened ones a guest would actually use, throw out the started ones, and send household backstock that drifted in here back to the bathroom it came from.

Two bins, not five. Guest supplies in one, cleaning products in the other, both light enough to lift out with one hand so the cabinet base stays visible. Toilet paper stacks on its own, where it can be seen the second the door opens, because a guest who is hunting for it will not come and ask.

Empty the cabinet completely and wipe the base, looking for dark rings or softened board that mean the trap has been weeping. Wipe the neck and cap of every bottle, since dried cleaner running down the side is what makes a cabinet sticky.

Poison, choke, or strangle: bowl cleaner and bleach sitting under this sink are at exactly the height of a visiting toddler who has been sent in to wash their hands alone. Either lift the cleaning bin to a high shelf elsewhere or fit the cabinet with a latch, and never let bleach share a bin with an acid limescale or bowl cleaner, because a loose cap on both is all it takes for them to meet.

Write the two bin labels by hand in plain words a guest can read, Guest Supplies and Cleaning, and draw a line on the shelf at the toilet paper minimum. When the stack falls below the line it goes on the shopping list, no counting required.
When you restock your own bathroom after a shop, open this cabinet on the same trip and build the toilet paper stack back up to the line.

zones.purpose: It has to be ready for someone to shower in tonight, even though nobody has used it since spring.
zones.done: Three bottles in the caddy, all recognizable and more than a third full, a curtain liner or glass screen with no pink film along the bottom edge, a bath mat folded over the tub rim rather than lying wet on the floor, and grout that is the same color in the corners as it is in the middle. A non-slip surface underfoot inside the tub.

steps.text: Take out every bottle and turn it over. This is where the household's rejected products retire: the shampoo nobody liked, the body wash that smells wrong, the conditioner welded to the shelf. Keep one shampoo, one conditioner, one body wash, all readable and more than a third full. The rest go, along with the old razor and the disintegrating loofah.

Hang the caddy or fit a corner shelf so nothing stands directly on the tub floor collecting water underneath it. A bar of soap gets a draining dish, never a puddle. Put a hook inside the door at a height someone can reach with wet hands and no glasses on.

Start with the mold, because it needs time you should not spend standing there: spray the grout lines and the bottom band of the curtain liner, go clean the rest of the room, then come back and rinse. A fabric liner goes in the washing machine rather than getting scrubbed by hand.

Fall: your guest is stepping into an unfamiliar tub, probably at night, on a surface they cannot judge the grip of. Put a non-slip mat or adhesive strips on the tub floor and make sure there is one thing solidly anchored to grab, because a towel bar screwed into drywall will tear straight out the moment it takes a person's weight.

Three bottles, one soap, one mat, one anchored grab point, and no personal items. If the shower has stood unused for a month, run it hot for a minute before a guest arrives, which clears the stale water sitting in the line and proves the drain is still running freely.
Whoever used it last squeegees the glass or shakes out the liner and drapes the bath mat over the tub rim. A liner left bunched against the tile is exactly where the pink film starts again.

zones.purpose: It has to be clean and stocked in a way that is obvious to someone who will never ask you where anything is.
zones.done: One spare roll standing in plain sight on the tank or in a holder a seated person can reach without standing up. A brush that is dry, resting in a holder with no liquid pooled in the bottom. A small trash can with a liner actually in it. No ring at the water line, and a dry, dust-free floor behind the pedestal.

steps.text: Clear everything from the top of the tank and the floor behind the bowl: the collection of air fresheners, the second brush, the magazines, the box of something nobody has identified in years. One reserve roll stays in the open. Nothing else.

Put the reserve roll where a seated person can reach it without getting up, since that is the entire point of a reserve roll. Set the brush and the trash can on the side away from the door swing so nobody kicks either one on the way in.

Treat the bowl first and let it sit under the rim and at the water line while you work outward: seat hinges, then the base of the pedestal, then the floor behind it, which is where splash and dust collect and where the smell in a guest bathroom actually comes from. Use a cloth in a color you use nowhere else in the house.

Poison, choke, or strangle: a bottle of bowl cleaner parked behind the pedestal sits at a crawling child's eye level, usually with the cap loose. It goes back in the cleaning bin with the cap tight every time. It never shares a shelf with bleach, because bleach and an acid bowl cleaner mixed in a small room with the door shut produce a gas that will drop a healthy adult.

One visible reserve roll, backstock in the cabinet, brush dry in its holder, liner in the can, no ring at the water line. Write those five lines on a card and stand it in the cleaning bin, so the person holding the brush reads the standard at the moment they are able to meet it.
When you carry the trash out on collection night, you are already standing here, so drop in a new liner and check that the reserve roll is still upright.

zones.purpose: It holds one complete fresh set of towels so hosting never starts with a search.
zones.done: One bundle per expected guest, each holding a bath towel, a hand towel, and a washcloth folded together, matching in color, smelling of nothing at all. A clean bath mat folded flat beneath the bundles. A hand's width of air above the stack. No thin gray towel kept for the dog sharing the shelf.

steps.text: Unfold every towel and look at it in daylight rather than closet light. Anything thin along the fold line, permanently gray, stiff from too much softener, or carrying a hair dye or nosebleed stain comes out of the guest stack. It becomes a rag or a car towel today. It does not go back just in case.

Store as complete sets rather than in stacks of like with like. Bath towel, hand towel, and washcloth folded into a single bundle so setting up for a visitor is one lift instead of three searches. Two bundles ready covers most households, and the bath mat lives underneath them.

Wash the stored set hot even though nobody has used it, because a towel that has sat folded in a closed closet all season carries a musty note that appears the instant it gets wet. Wipe the shelf, then run your hand along the back wall of the closet, since damp there is what the towels have been drinking.

Burn or fire: if this closet also holds the water heater, towels pressed against the tank, a hot pipe, or the heater's cable are a scorch and fire risk that no amount of neat folding fixes. Leave a hand's width of clearance around anything that gets hot, and never let a stack lean on the unit or trap its cable behind it.

Two complete bundles on the marked shelf with the bath mat beneath, and a mark on the shelf edge showing where the second bundle ends. When one is missing, the gap reads as a gap without anyone counting.
When a guest leaves and you strip the bed, the used bathroom set goes straight into that same wash, and the shelf gets restocked before the sheets are dry.

zones.purpose: Run loads reliably, and stay maintained well enough that the machines are never the reason laundry stops.
zones.done: Both drums empty with the washer door propped ajar, nothing at all sitting on either lid, a clean lint screen back in its slot, and a strip of masking tape on the side of the dryer with the month you last cleared the duct written on it.

steps.text: Clear the tops of both machines and the inside of both drums. The single sock behind the agitator, the hardened box of dryer sheets, the bottle of softener you stopped using: all of it comes off the machines now rather than being shuffled sideways.

Machine lids carry nothing. Put the vent brush and the pack of machine cleaner tablets on the shelf above, so the lids open freely and a knocked cap cannot roll down behind the drum where nobody retrieves it.

Lift the folds of the door gasket and wipe out the coins, hairpins, and grey slime that collect in there. Wash the detergent drawer in the sink, then run a hot cycle with a cleaner tablet in the empty drum.

Clear the lint screen every single load, then check the duct behind the dryer for the soft grey packing that builds where the pipe bends. Lint plus heat is a fire, and a crushed foil accordion duct traps far more of it than a smooth rigid pipe does.

Write the month on masking tape stuck to the side of the dryer each time you clear the duct, so the next check is a glance instead of an argument with your memory. A standard is the best way you know today, written down.
When the dryer buzzer sounds, the lint screen gets cleared before the door closes again. That one motion, every load, is the whole machine standard.

zones.purpose: Hold the chemistry that actually gets used, at a dose you can measure and out of a child's reach.
zones.done: One working detergent, one bleach, one tub of oxygen powder and one stain treatment standing on a wipeable tray, the pod tub latched and above shoulder height, the true dose line inked on the cap, and not one unlabeled bottle on the shelf.

steps.text: Line every bottle, stick, spray and pod tub up on the floor. Anything crusted shut at the neck, anything with the label washed off, and anything bought for one stain that already came out goes to the disposal pile. Two open jugs of the same detergent become one jug in use and one refill.

The everyday detergent and its dosing cap sit within arm's reach of the open washer lid, because that is where you use them. Bleach and the stain sprays go behind them on a tray, and the pod tub goes higher than a child can reach on tiptoe from an upturned laundry basket.

Detergent drips, always. Wipe the spigot on the jug and the shelf under it, then stand every container on a shallow tray so the next drip lands on plastic you can rinse rather than a shelf that stays tacky for a year.

Bleach and any ammonia based cleaner never share a shelf, and never share a bucket. The pod tub gets a latched lid or a high shelf without exception, because a detergent pod looks exactly like a sweet to a toddler and bursts in the mouth.

Mark the true dose line on the cap with a permanent marker, since the moulded cap is bigger than the dose almost every time. Write the job on the tray edge under each bottle, wash, whites, stains, so a returned bottle lands back in its own footprint.
When you pour the last dose out of a jug, the empty goes straight to recycling and the replacement goes on the shopping list before you press start on that load.

zones.purpose: Turn dirty clothes into loads that can go straight into the machine without being handled twice.
zones.done: Three labeled bags standing clear of the walking line, each below half full, a small dish on the shelf holding nothing older than today, and bare floor in front of the washer door.

steps.text: Empty every hamper and see what a real week actually produces: whites, darks, towels, delicates, work clothes. Any stream that never fills on its own gets merged into another, and the spare hampers you were holding for those streams leave the room.

One bag per stream, standing where clothes are actually taken off rather than where the bags happen to fit. Add a small dish on the shelf for pocket contents, because coins, hair ties and the occasional memory stick need somewhere to land that is not the drum.
Damp gym kit is what makes a hamper smell, not dirt. Wipe the inside of each bin while it is empty, and never let a wet towel spend the night in a lined bag with the lid down.

A hamper parked on a landing or at the top of a step is a fall you take with your arms full and your view blocked. Keep the bags out of the walking line entirely, and never carry a basket loaded higher than your eyeline.
Label each bag with the load it makes rather than the colour it holds: hot towels, cold darks, gentle. Anyone in the house can then start a machine without asking which setting the bag wants.
Pockets get checked as the item goes into the bag, not later at the machine. That dish on the shelf is where a lip balm stops being a whole ruined load.

zones.purpose: Turn a finished dry load into clothes that are back in drawers the same day.
zones.done: A counter bare enough to roll pastry on, one empty basket per bedroom stacked underneath it, six spare hangers on the rail at the end, and no clean clothing anywhere in the room.

steps.text: Clear the counter right down, including everything that was never laundry: the post, the toolbox, the parcel waiting to be returned, the vase from Christmas. Whatever is parked here is the reason a dry load goes back in for a second tumble.

Keep one basket per person or per bedroom under the counter, so folding and delivering are the same motion rather than two separate jobs. Hangers live on a rail at the end, not in a tangled heap you have to unpick before you can use one.
Wipe the counter before you fold, not after. Clean clothes pick up whatever detergent dust and lint the last load shed here, and a folding board skates badly over grit.

If you iron on this counter, the iron gets one heatproof rest and the cord runs behind it where no arm can hook through. When you step away, unplug at the wall rather than trusting the switch or the auto shutoff.

The counter is either completely empty or holding exactly one load in progress. There is no third state. Photograph it empty and tape the photo inside the cupboard door so nobody has to guess what clear means.

Tip the basket out onto the counter rather than setting it down full. A full basket on the floor keeps its clothes for another day, while a heap on the counter gets dealt with before anyone can use the surface again.

zones.purpose: Dry the few things a hot drum would ruin, and get them off the rack the moment they are dry.
zones.done: The rack folded flat against the wall with dry bars, its drip tray wiped out and empty, the rail holding six spare hangers, and nothing hanging that was washed before today.

steps.text: Strip the rack completely. Anything still damp goes back on, anything dry goes to its drawer right now, and the wool jumper that has been draped over the end rung since spring either goes away properly or leaves the house.

The rack gets one spot with a drip tray underneath, not wherever the last load abandoned it. Hang bras, wool and swimwear on the top rungs where air actually moves, and keep the bottom rungs for flat items that can take the slower dry.

A rack that is stored damp grows a musty smell and passes it straight to the next load hung on it. Wipe the bars dry when you strip it, and fold it flat so both faces get air rather than pressing wet metal against wet metal.

Water on a hard floor under a drying rack is a slip you take in socks with an armful of laundry. Keep the drip tray in place, and never stand the rack where drips can reach a wall outlet or a plugged in extension lead running along the skirting.

The rack is either in use holding one set of damp items, or folded flat against the wall. Nothing has permanent residence on the rungs, and no garment starts a second night up there without a reason you could say out loud.
Before you open the washer to start the next load, you clear the rack. Anything dry comes off first, which means the rack is always ready for the load you are about to run.

zones.purpose: Hold the tools that keep this room and the strip of floor in front of the machines clean, dry and ready.
zones.done: Broom, mop and dustpan hanging heads up with painted outlines showing behind each one, a single labeled caddy holding every vacuum attachment, a mop head that is dry to the touch, and the bucket sitting inside its taped floor square with nothing stored inside it.

steps.text: Stand every tool up in the open: the broom, the mop, the dustpan, the vacuum hose and its attachments, the sack of rags. Two brooms become one broom. The crevice tool that fits no vacuum you still own goes out today.

Hang the broom, mop and dustpan on a wall rail with the heads uppermost and clear of the floor, because bristles resting on concrete splay and then re-soil the floor they touch. Vacuum attachments live in one labeled caddy, so a missing one is visible rather than assumed.

Rinse the mop head and hang it to dry before it goes back on the rail, and empty the vacuum canister before you store it. A mop put away wet and grey spreads that water back down the next floor it touches.

A broom handle leaned against the wall behind a door swings and falls at head height the moment the door opens. Everything is hung or in a bin, nothing leans. Drain cleaner and bleach in this corner sit on a shelf above the mop bucket, never inside it where a rinse could mix them.

Paint or tape an outline behind each hook so a missing tool shows from the doorway, and give the bucket a taped square of floor that belongs to it alone. The room then reports its own state without anyone opening a cupboard.
When you clear the lint screen at the end of a wash day, sweep the strip of floor in front of the machines with the broom that is already hanging an arm's length away.

zones.purpose: One clear surface for the work you are actually doing right now.
zones.done: The monitor, keyboard, and mouse in fixed positions, one notebook, one inbox tray holding fewer than a dozen sheets, no sticky notes on the monitor bezel, and the power strip hooked off the floor so the chair rolls over bare carpet.

steps.text: Take everything off the surface and onto the floor, then put back only what the task in front of you needs, plus the inbox tray. The dead pens, the second mug, and the fringe of sticky notes around the screen do not go back up.
Keyboard square in front of the monitor, notebook on your writing-hand side, phone face down beyond it, and the whole sweep the mouse travels left bare so you are never steering around a stapler.
Power down, wipe the screen with cleaner sprayed onto the microfiber cloth, then do the desk edge and the underside lip where your forearms rest, which is the grubbiest part of the whole room.
Lift the power strip off the floor onto a hook on the desk leg, and check that no charging cable crosses the arc the chair rolls through. Your feet should find nothing under there.
Photograph the cleared desk and tape the print inside the top drawer, so the word clear stops being a matter of opinion in this household.

When you shut the laptop lid at the end of the working day, reset the surface to match the photo before you stand up. Doing it next morning is too late, because by then the pile has been sitting there since last night and reads as normal.

zones.purpose: Hold the small tools you reach for without looking, and the live files you touch weekly.
zones.done: A top drawer with a divided tray holding pens that all write, one stapler, one pair of scissors point-down in its own slot, and a deep pedestal drawer of hanging files with tabs all standing in one line.

steps.text: Tip the top drawer onto the cleared desk and test every pen on scrap paper. Dried highlighters, bent paperclips, loose staples, dead batteries, and chargers whose device you cannot point at in this house all go now.

Daily hand tools live in the divided tray up top, hanging files fill the deep pedestal drawer, and the two never mix. The stapler does not end up riding on the folders, and no folder gets laid flat across the pens.
Vacuum the drawer bottoms, which collect eraser crumbs, loose staples, and paperclip fuzz, then wipe the runners so the drawer closes without a shove.
Scissors and the letter opener get their own slot with points facing the back of the drawer, because you reach into this drawer blind while looking at the screen.
Write what each drawer front holds, in the words this house actually uses, so tape and stamps are found without pulling three drawers.
When you sit down to pay the household bills, put back into the drawers anything that migrated out onto the desk that week.

zones.purpose: Keep the documents you are genuinely required to hold, and put your hand on any one of them without opening a second drawer.
zones.done: Hanging folders labelled by the question you would ask when looking, tabs all in the same position so your eye runs one straight line, a closed fireproof box holding the permanent originals, and a full shred bag by the door ready to go.

steps.text: Work one drawer at a time into three piles: keep as paper, scan then shred, shred now. Tax paper by year, warranties and manuals only for machines still in this house, and no folder for anything the issuer will reprint on request.
File by the question you will ask when you go hunting, so "car", "house", "health", "school", rather than by document type. Nobody has ever gone looking for a folder called Correspondence.
Filing is where you inspect: check the drawer bottom for damp, look for silverfish, and photograph any thermal receipt that has started to fade before the print disappears entirely.
Get the permanent originals out of a cardboard box on top of the cabinet and into a closed fireproof box at floor level, and keep the paper mass away from the power strip and any heater.

Write your retention rule on a card and tape it inside the top drawer, naming which categories are permanent, which run by tax year, and which get scanned. A standard is the best way you know today, written down.
When the new tax paperwork arrives each year, that is the signal to pull and shred the oldest year that has passed your retention period. One in, one out, and the drawer never overflows again.

zones.purpose: Hold the reference you genuinely reach for, at the height you reach for it from.
zones.done: Working reference at seated eye level from the desk chair, heavy binders and box files on the bottom two shelves, a bookend closing each group, a hand's width of empty shelf left at the end of every row, and the unit screwed to the wall.

steps.text: Take every book, binder, and manual off the shelves. Appliance manuals for machines that left the house, superseded editions with a year in the title, and binders from projects that finished all go out in one pass.
Group by why you reach: working reference at eye level from where you sit, occasional reading at standing height, archive boxes highest, heavy binders lowest.
Dust from the top shelf down with a dry cloth, wipe the front edge of each shelf, and vacuum the top edges of the books themselves, which is where the dust in this room actually settles.
Screw the unit into the wall studs, and move the box files, binders, and any framed glass award off the high shelf that sits above where your head is when you are working.

A bookend closes every group, and a hand's width of empty shelf stays at the end of each row. When a shelf has no slack left, that is the visible signal that a book has to leave, not that you need another shelf.
When you finish a book or close out a project binder, it does not go back on the shelf by reflex. It gets the keep-or-go question at that moment, while the answer is still obvious.

zones.purpose: Turn paper into files and files into paper, without hunting for either.
zones.done: Paper in a bin directly beneath the printer with a min line and a max line drawn inside it, one spare cartridge in a labelled box beside it, a single scan tray with a to-do side and a done side, clear air behind the machine, and nothing sitting on the lid.

steps.text: Keep only ink or toner that matches the model number on the printer currently plugged in. The half reams of odd paper, the letterhead with the old address, and the envelopes from two houses ago go out.

Paper goes directly under the printer, the spare cartridge in a labelled box beside it, and the scan pile gets one tray with a to-do side and a done side, so you can tell at a glance what has already been through the glass.

Powered off, lift the lid and clean the scanner glass with cleaner on the cloth, never sprayed onto the glass where it can run inside. Use a dry cloth for toner dust and vacuum the paper lint around the feed tray.

Leave clear air at the back of the machine, because the fuser runs genuinely hot, and plug the printer straight into a wall outlet rather than into a strip chained off another strip. Nothing sits on top of the lid, not the plant and not your drink.
Draw a min line and a max line inside the paper bin. When the stack drops to the min line, the next ream goes on the shopping list that day, not the day it runs out mid-job.
When you pull the last sheet from the bin, refill it from the shelf before you walk away from the machine, while you are already standing there.

zones.purpose: Hold the consumables this office genuinely burns through in a year, and no more.
zones.done: One open pack of each consumable at hand height with its backstock directly behind it, reams of paper on the bottom shelf, min and max written on a card at the front edge of each shelf, and a step stool standing in the corner of the room.

steps.text: Bring everything out and line it up on the floor in categories so you can see the true count, because a dozen packs of sticky notes look like nothing until they stand side by side. Dried glue sticks, dead markers, cracked folders, and adapters nobody can identify leave.

One open pack of each consumable at hand height, its backstock immediately behind it on the same shelf, so restocking the pen tray is a single reach rather than a hunt through three boxes of envelopes.
Wipe the shelves and check for a pen that has leaked, a split toner pouch, or the sticky ring under a roll of tape that has gone soft.
Reams of paper and boxes of envelopes are heavy and they belong on the bottom shelf, not overhead. Put an actual step stool in this room and stop standing on the rolling chair to reach the top shelf.
Write min and max on a card at the front edge of each shelf, so a low stock is visible from the doorway and anyone in the house can read the cabinet without asking you.
When you open the last pack of something, it goes onto the household shopping list on the fridge before you break the seal, not after it runs out.

zones.purpose: The one surface in the house where things get fixed, glued, cut, and assembled.
zones.done: A bare bench top holding only the vise and the task light, one tray with the current job in it, clamps racked on the rail, and swept concrete visible under the bench.

steps.text: Clear the top down to bare wood. Every screw living in a jar lid, every glue bottle with a plugged nozzle, and every offcut you saved because the grain looked too good to bin gets a verdict before anything is allowed back up.

Give the vise its own corner and keep a full arm's length of open top in front of it, because that is the space a long board swings through. Clamps go on the rail within reach and fasteners in the drawer directly beneath. The post that comes in, the half-tin of paint, and the parcel waiting to go back are not bench items and never were.
Vacuum sawdust and metal filings out of the bench dog holes and the seam where the top meets the back wall, then wipe the vise screw down and put a drop of oil on it.

Check the bench outlet and the task light cord for nicks, and confirm you can plug the sander in without a lead crossing the strip of floor you stand on. Chisels and utility blades never rest edge-up on the top, where a hand sweeps sawdust without looking.

Tape a photo of the cleared bench, vise and task light and nothing else, on the wall directly behind it at eye height. When you look up and see a paint tin or a coil of wire that the photo does not show, that is the next thing to leave.

A project is not over when the glue sets. It is over when the clamps are back on the rail, the offcuts are in the scrap bin, and the top is swept, and all of that happens before the task light goes off.

zones.purpose: Keeps the tools you reach for weekly visible, findable, and provably all present.
zones.done: Every hand tool hanging on its own drawn outline with no blank silhouettes, one hammer and one adjustable wrench at chest height nearest the door, saw teeth sheathed, and the cabinet latched.

steps.text: Pull every hammer, screwdriver, plier, and wrench onto one sheet on the floor and count the duplicates honestly. Pliers rusted shut, wrenches with rounded jaws, and drivers with chewed tips are scrap metal, not spares, and keeping them means hunting past them forever.

Hang by how often your hand reaches, not by tool family. Tape measure, utility knife, and the number two driver go at chest height nearest the door, because those three come off the wall for jobs that take under a minute. Pipe wrenches and socket sets sit lower and further along.
Wipe each tool with an oiled rag as it goes back up, and wipe the pegboard behind it. Rust starts at the handle end, where hands leave salt.

Handsaws and chisels get a sheath or a blade guard before they touch the wall. Seat every pegboard hook properly, because a heavy wrench knocked off a shallow hook lands on a foot, and put a latch on the low cabinet if children ever come out here.
Trace the silhouette of every tool onto the board in marker or paint. An empty outline tells you the tenon saw is missing without you having to remember that you own one.
The driver goes back on its outline before you fold the step ladder away, not at the weekend. A tool that spends the night on the bench top is one the wall has already started to lose.

zones.purpose: Holds the powered tools, their packs, and their chargers so a tool is always ready to run and nothing is left charging unattended.
zones.done: One shelf per battery system with its charger mounted at the front edge and no pack sitting on it, every drill and saw in its case or on a labelled hook with guards down, and bits, blades, and sanding discs in the shallow drawer underneath.

steps.text: Line every pack up and run it in the tool it belongs to until you know which ones still hold a charge. Packs that die in a minute, chargers for the drill you sold, and the sander with the taped cord all leave today.

Group by battery system rather than by task, so one shelf carries the tools, packs, and charger of a single platform and you stop carrying a green pack to a red tool. Blades, drill bits, and sanding discs go in a shallow drawer directly beneath the tools that take them.

Brush or blow the motor vents on each drill and saw clear of packed dust, and clean the battery contacts and the charger terminals. A vent clogged with plaster dust runs a motor hot enough to shorten its life.

Packs come off the charger once they are full and sit at partial charge on a shelf well clear of the fuel can and the rag bin. Confirm every blade guard springs back freely on its own, and retire any tool with a cracked case rather than pushing it behind the others.
One shelf label per battery system, charger mounted at the front edge, so a pack left charging shows as a lump on the shelf edge you can see from the doorway without walking in.
Pulling a full pack off the charger is part of finishing the job, the same as putting the drill back in its case. Nothing sleeps on a charger, whatever the manual claims about smart cut-off.

zones.purpose: Keeps the fluids, cables, and cleaning kit for the cars you actually own upright, labelled, and separate from everything the household touches.
zones.done: Every fluid bottle standing upright on a clean drip tray with its opened date written on the shoulder, jumper cables and tyre gauge together in one bag by the door, rags in a closed metal can, and not a single bottle for a car nobody here drives.

steps.text: Line every bottle up and read the label out loud. Oil in a weight your current engine does not take, coolant for the van you sold, and the half bottle whose label has soaked away into unreadable grey all come out of the row.

Fluids stand upright on a shallow drip tray at waist height, where a weeping cap shows as a ring rather than soaking into a shelf. Jumper cables, tyre gauge, and lug wrench live together in one bag right by the door, because you go for those with a dead engine, in the dark, in a hurry.

Wipe every bottle shoulder and check the tray for the ring that says something is seeping. Wash the wash mitts and microfibre towels on their own, never with house laundry, so grit and old wax stay out of the good towels.

Petrol and any can that has ever held it stays out of the house envelope, capped tight, and never on a shelf near the water heater's pilot flame. Polish and oil rags go into a metal can with a lid, not the plastic bin.

Label the tray shelf with exactly what belongs on it, and mark every bottle with the month you opened it. Brake fluid pulls water out of the air and coolant goes off once the seal is broken, and the date is the only way you will ever know which is which.
You already lift the bonnet to check the oil. While it is up, look along the tray for a fresh ring, and an empty bottle goes straight into the bin instead of back into the row.

zones.purpose: Holds the gear for the sports this household currently plays, with the in-season kit easiest to grab.
zones.done: Bikes on wall hooks with bare floor beneath them, one labelled bin per activity, this season's kit at the front of the shelf, and every helmet in the garage belonging to a head that still wears it.

steps.text: Carry every helmet, ball, racket, and pair of cleats out onto the driveway and match each one to a person who plays that sport now. Cleats a size too small and the paddle from that one river trip do not come back through the door.

Bikes hang on wall hooks nearest the door so nobody unhooks three to get one out on a Saturday morning. Balls go in a tall bin or a bungee-front rack rather than loose on the floor where they roll under the car, and this season's kit sits at the front of the shelf with the off-season behind it.

Air out and wipe down helmet liners and shin pads, hose the mud off cleats and dry them right through before they go back, and leave the cooler propped open with a rag of baking soda inside so it does not come out smelling of last summer.

A helmet that has taken one real impact is finished even if the shell looks perfect, and so is one past the date moulded inside it. Overhead bike hooks must be rated and driven into studs, never drywall anchors, and never hung where a car door swings open into a hanging wheel.
One labelled bin per activity, and the label carries the sport plus the name of the person it belongs to. Gear that fits no named bin has no owner in this house and does not stay in it.
The front and back of the shelf trade places the first weekend you turn the heating on, and again the first weekend you leave the windows open all day.

zones.purpose: Stores the yard tools and outdoor supplies so long handles stay off the floor and garden chemicals stay latched away from everything else.
zones.done: Every long-handled tool hanging head-up on the rail with nothing leaning in a corner, the hose coiled on its reel beside the door it goes out of, and all garden chemicals in their original labelled containers behind a latch above head height.

steps.text: Out go the rake with three tines left, the hose with the split you have meant to patch for two summers, and the cracked nursery pots kept for seedlings you never started. Count your spades honestly, because most garages hold four and dig with one.

Long handles hang head-up on a rail so no fork stands loose in a corner waiting to be trodden on. The hose lives on a reel beside the door it goes out of, not coiled on the slab. Fertiliser, weed killer, and seed share one shelf with a lip on it, well away from the cooler and anything else that touches food or skin.

Scrape caked soil off the spade and hoe blades, wipe them with an oily rag, and run a file along the spade edge so it bites next time. Empty and rinse the spreader hopper, because leftover fertiliser eats the metal from the inside out over a winter.

Garden chemicals stay in their original labelled containers on a latched shelf above child and pet height, never decanted into a drink bottle. String trimmers and hedge shears go up with guards fitted and cutting ends pointing away from the aisle you walk down.

A painted or taped strip on the wall behind each long handle, so a bare strip is a question you answer before you close the door. One sign on the chemical shelf reading "garden chemicals only, nothing else on this shelf."
The mower needs to cool before it goes away anyway, and that is the window when the spade gets scraped, wiped, and hung back on its strip, instead of being found rusted solid next spring.

zones.purpose: Holds the things you genuinely need once or twice a year, high up and out of the way, without becoming the place decisions go to hide.
zones.done: Every overhead bin labelled in letters you can read standing on the slab, a last-opened month and year on the end of each one, the heaviest bins on the lowest rack, nothing overhanging the parking bay, and a small map taped beside the light switch.

steps.text: Bring the bins down to the floor before you judge them, because nobody sorts honestly from the third step of a ladder with one arm through a lid. Start with the holiday bin that has not come down in three Decembers and the box marked "misc".

Heavy bins go on the lowest rack and light bulky things, folding chairs and the artificial tree, go highest. Group by the time of year they come down, so one December trip up the ladder brings the lights, the tree, and the wrapping bin down together.

Wipe the lids. The depth of dust on an overhead lid tells you exactly how many years it has been since anything came out of that bin. While you are up there, look at the rack underside and the ceiling above it for the brown stain that means the roof is letting water in.

Nothing goes overhead that you cannot lift down with both hands on a stable ladder, and nothing you might need in the dark or in a hurry. Check that the rack bolts land in joists, not just in the plasterboard, and that loaded bins sit fully inside the rails rather than overhanging the roof of a parked car.

Every bin gets a large label you can read from the slab plus the month and year it was last opened. A map taped beside the light switch says which bay holds what, so nobody climbs a ladder simply to find out.

The moment a bin is on the floor with its lid off, write the new month and year on the end before it goes back up. A bin whose newest date is two Decembers old comes down and gets opened at the next clear-out rather than being lifted straight back.

zones.purpose: The one surface where a project actually gets built, cut, glued, and repaired.
zones.done: A bare bench top except the vise and the task lamp, one project tray holding the current job's parts, and a clear run of bench in front of the vise long enough to lay a board across. Every chisel and square back on its traced outline, the dog holes empty, and no offcuts or glue squeeze-out under the bench.

steps.text: Clear the bench top and the shelf beneath it completely, then give every half-finished project a verdict: back on the bench with a date, or broken down into parts and stock. Snapped blades, glue bottles gone solid, and brackets you cannot identify leave now.

Hang the tools your hand reaches for mid-cut, the marking knife, the combination square, the block plane, within arm's reach of the vise, and put everything you use once a project on the wall behind. Traced silhouettes mean a missing chisel shows up before you finish vacuuming.

Vacuum the bench top and the dog holes rather than brushing them out, then scrape dried glue drips off the surface before they telegraph into the next workpiece. Wipe the vise screw and give it a drop of oil.

Check the vise jaws still bite a test piece without slipping, and move the lamp cord so it does not lie across the part of the bench a handsaw crosses. A chisel lying edge up in an open tray is what your hand finds when you reach across the bench without looking.

Trace the outlines on the tool wall in permanent marker so a gap reads as a missing chisel, then take one photo of the cleared bench and tape it at eye level where you stand, because that photo is what bare means here.
The last part of every session is the bench clear down, done before you take your safety glasses off, because once the glasses come off you are finished for the day and you know it.

zones.purpose: Keep every corded and cordless tool guarded, complete with its own accessories, and ready to pick up and use.
zones.done: Each tool in a labeled home with its guard closed and its blade wrench or chuck key attached to it, not floating in a drawer. Batteries sitting on a shelf off the chargers, no bare circular saw blade loose in a drawer, and no cord repaired with electrical tape anywhere in the zone.

steps.text: Line up the duplicates and be honest about the second drill and the sander you replaced but kept. Battery packs that no longer hold a charge through one job are not spares, they are recycling, and taped cords are not tools.

Store each tool with the parts that make it usable: the circular saw with its rip fence and blade wrench, the router with its collet spanners and the bits it actually takes. Hunting for a collet spanner is how a router ends up used without one.
Blow or brush the motor vents clear of packed sawdust, take the pitch off saw blades with resin remover so they stop burning cuts, and pull the clogged sanding pads.

Work the retracting guard on every saw with your thumb and confirm it snaps back on its own; a sticky guard is the injury waiting in this zone. Flex each cord at the strain relief where the sheath cracks first, and never leave a corded tool stored plugged in.
Label each tool's home on the wall or the shelf edge, and set one charge rule for the batteries: partial charge, off the charger when the job ends, resting on a shelf that is not wood.
When a battery goes onto the charger at the end of a job, the tool it came off goes onto its hook in the same motion. The two actions travel together or neither happens.

zones.purpose: Let you put your hand on the right screw straight away, so a project never stops for a hardware run.
zones.done: One fastener type and size per compartment, with a sample screw glued to the outside of each drawer face so you match by eye rather than by reading. Deck screws separate from drywall screws, no coffee tin of mixed hardware anywhere on the shelf, and a marked minimum line inside the compartments you empty most.

steps.text: Empty the mixed jars onto a tray and keep only what you can name confidently by size and type. Rusted screws, bent nails, and the anchors that came free with a shelf you no longer own are not a stock of hardware.

Sort by type first and size second, with the sizes you drive weekly at hand height and the specialty hinges and threaded rod up high. The sample fastener on the drawer face is the label that still works when your hands are dusty.
Vacuum the drawers of metal filings and grit, and look for rust bloom in the bottom corners; if you find it, the cabinet is against a cold outside wall and needs moving before you refill it.

A wall cabinet full of steel fasteners is far heavier than it looks, so fix it into studs rather than plasterboard anchors before you load it. Spilled screws on a concrete floor put you on your back holding something sharp.
One compartment per size, no exceptions and no shared drawers, with a minimum line marked inside so a low bin announces itself the moment you slide it open.
The handful of leftover fasteners in your pocket goes back into its compartment before the tools go back on the wall, or into the scrap metal tin if you cannot name it.

zones.purpose: Hold the wood and metal you will genuinely use, stored so it stays straight and does not fall on anyone.
zones.done: Boards lying flat and supported along their length with the longest and heaviest at the bottom, sheet goods standing on edge against the wall rather than leaning out into the room, and an offcut bin with its size floor written on the front in marker. Nothing stored directly on the floor, and the route from the bench to the door clear along its full width.

steps.text: Take the offcut bin apart piece by piece against a written size floor. Twisted or badly cupped boards, anything with hidden nails or an unknown coating, and pressure treated scrap all leave, and the coated stock does not go on the fire.

Group by length and thickness so you can pull a board without unstacking three others, put pipe, trim, and dowel upright in a vertical bin, and support flat stock at intervals close enough that nothing sags between brackets.
Sweep out the gap behind the rack where sawdust, spider webs, and mouse droppings collect out of sight, then wipe surface rust off steel stock and give it a light oil before it goes back.

Fix the rack into structural framing, not just the wall skin, and load it heaviest at the bottom. A full sheet of ply leaning at too shallow an angle will slide flat without warning, and it will take out whatever is in front of it.
Mark the lengths on the rack rails so stock returns to the right bay, write the size floor on the offcut bin, and mark a fill line above which the bin is full and the shortest piece leaves.
Before you unplug the saw at the end of a cutting session, every offcut goes either into the bin or into the fire bucket. Not onto the bench, not onto the floor, not on top of the rack.

zones.purpose: Store paint, glue, stain, and solvent so they stay usable and so they never start a fire.
zones.done: Every product in its original labeled container inside a closed metal cabinet, each lid dated in marker, water based paint on one shelf and solvents and thinners on another.
