Oily rags in a self-closing metal can with the lid down, a drip tray under the solvent shelf, and no aerosol standing on a sunny sill or near a pilot light.

steps.text: Open and judge each container. Paint with a thick skin or a sour smell is finished, wood glue that has gone stringy or granular will not hold a joint, and cured polyurethane in a half bottle is a rock. Take all of it to household hazardous waste, never the bin, never the drain.

Separate what should never meet: solvents and thinners on their own shelf, water based finishes on another, and hardeners kept away from the resins they cure. Keep the stir sticks and the brushes for each family with them.
Wipe the rim of every can before the lid goes back on, because a rim full of dried finish is why the can skins over. Clean brushes right through to the ferrule and wipe down the spill tray.

A rag soaked in oil finish generates its own heat as it cures and can ignite with nothing touching it, so it goes in a lidded metal can or gets spread flat outdoors to dry. Keep flammable liquids away from any pilot light or heater, and ventilate before you spray, not after.

Date every container with a marker the day it arrives, and write the shelf layout on the inside of the cabinet door so the solvents and the water based finishes stay apart even when you are putting things away in a hurry.
When you wash out a brush at the end of a finishing job, that is when the can gets its date checked and the rag goes into the metal can.

zones.purpose: Make protective gear so easy to reach that putting it on is faster than skipping it.
zones.done: Safety glasses on hooks at the door you come in through, one labeled pair per regular user, hearing protection beside them, and dust masks in a dated box. An extinguisher mounted on the wall with its gauge in the green and clear floor in front of it, and a first aid kit that still has burn dressings and more than three plasters in it.

steps.text: Scratched, hazed safety glasses are the reason people stop wearing safety glasses, so bin them. Perished gloves, respirator cartridges past their date, and a first aid kit you have quietly been raiding for household plasters all get replaced rather than rearranged.

Hang the gear at the door on the path you walk in, not on the far wall past the bench, and sized to the actual people who work here. Silhouettes behind each item show at a glance which pair is missing.
Wash the lenses in soap and water rather than wiping them on a dusty shop rag, which is what scratches them in the first place. Wipe the sweat and sawdust off the earmuff cushions so they still seal.

Lift the extinguisher, check the gauge sits in the green, and confirm nothing has crept into the space in front of it. Then put your hand on the shop's power cutoff and confirm you could reach it with sawdust in your eyes and the lights off.
Put an inspection date on masking tape on the extinguisher bracket and the first aid kit lid, and hang your safety glasses over the plug of the saw so you cannot power up without handling them first.
The gear goes back on the board as you switch off the shop light, never into a drawer or a jacket pocket, so the next person to walk in finds a full board.

zones.purpose: Holds the coats and bags that leave in the morning and come back the same evening.
zones.done: Two coats and one bag per person, each on their own named column, the lowest hooks set at the height of the shortest person in the house, and bare floor along the whole run of wall beneath them.

steps.text: Take every coat, bag, hat and scarf off the wall into one pile and hand each item to its owner to keep or release. Anything nobody has worn since the last change of season leaves the door and goes up to a wardrobe.

Give each person a vertical strip of wall rather than a shared rail, and set their hooks at their own reach so a child never has to ask for their coat. Bag on the lower hook, coat on the upper, so a backpack is never lifted over a wet jacket.
Wipe the rail and the wall behind it where shoulders and sleeves leave a grey smear, then vacuum the narrow strip of floor directly under the hooks where hood fluff and door grit gather.

A hook carrying four wet coats will pull a screw straight out of plasterboard, so check that every hook sits in a stud or a proper anchor before you reload the wall. Keep scarves, cords and drawstrings off the lowest hooks where a small child plays alone.
Write each name on its column at that person's eye height, and say the limit out loud so everyone hears it: one coat, one bag, one hat. A standard is the best way you know today, written down.
When you hang your own coat up at the end of the day, look along the wall and move anything sitting on the wrong column back to its owner's.

zones.purpose: Somewhere to sit while you deal with your footwear, and a brief stop for things genuinely on their way out of the house.
zones.done: A bare seat wide enough for two people to lace boots at once, no more than three objects on the surface, and one labelled basket at the end holding only what is leaving tomorrow.

steps.text: Clear the bench down to bare wood in one go. Most of what is on it belongs in another room, so carry those things there now rather than sliding them to the far end, where they will sit for another month.

Protect the seat itself as empty space and give the strays one outbound basket: the library books, the parcel to return, the form waiting for a signature. Nothing that lives in this house permanently gets to sit on this bench.
Wipe the seat and the front edge where boot heels scuff it, then pull the bench away from the wall and sweep out the drift of grit, receipts and single socks underneath.

Nothing heavy stores on a shelf above the seat, because a bike helmet or a paint tin landing on someone bent over a bootlace is exactly how that shelf fails. Keep the seat clear enough to actually sit on, because balancing on one leg to pull off a wet boot is how people go down.

Three objects maximum on the surface, and the outbound basket empties on the next trip out of the door. Photograph the cleared bench and tape the picture inside the nearest cupboard door as the reference.
When you sit down to change your shoes, take one thing off the bench into the house with you as you stand up.

zones.purpose: Holds the footwear actually being worn this season, and gives wet pairs somewhere to drain without soaking the floor.
zones.done: Two pairs per person on the rack, soles down and toes out, one lipped tray by the door holding whatever came in wet, and clear floor between the tray and the doorway.

steps.text: Bring every pair in the house down to this floor and match them up. Outgrown pairs, split soles and unmatched singles leave today, and anything for the opposite season goes up to its owner's wardrobe rather than back on the rack.

One row per person, heaviest boots on the bottom row so nobody lifts them, lightest slippers on top. Cleats and caked walking boots live on the tray only, never on a shelf where the dried mud drops onto the pair below.

Tip the tray out into the garden and wash it, because dried mud on a boot tray turns to dust and gets walked straight back inside. Wipe the rack rails and vacuum the floor of the rack where the grit lands.

A wet boot sole on a hard floor is the surest slip in this house, so the tray sits exactly where boots actually come off, not two steps further in. Keep the line from the door to the bench completely empty, because a shoe left out in a dark hallway is what people fall over at night.
Two pairs per person at the door, wet on the tray, dry on the rack. Mark the tray's footprint on the floor with tape so it goes back to the same spot after every clean.
When you take your boots off, they go soles down on the tray, and when they are dry they move up to the shelf that evening.

zones.purpose: Everything the animal needs to get out of the door, and everything you need when it comes back through it filthy.
zones.done: Lead clipped to collar on one hook with a full roll of waste bags attached, an old towel folded within arm's reach of the door, food sealed in a bin with the scoop inside it, and every treatment behind a closed door above the animal's nose and above a toddler's reach.

steps.text: Lay out every lead, collar, harness and chewed toy you can find in this room. Keep the lead you genuinely walk with plus one spare, then let the outgrown collar, the harness that never fitted and the retired long line go.

Hang the walking kit as one connected unit, lead clipped to collar with the bag roll threaded on, so leaving the house is one grab and not a search of three rooms. Towel on top of the food bin, treats up high where a nose cannot reach them.

Wash the scoop and wipe the crumbs and oils out of the bin before you refill it, rather than tipping fresh food onto stale, and put the paw towel through the wash with the door mats so one load covers both.

Flea, tick and worming treatments are poison to a child and to an animal of the wrong size, so they live in a closed box above reach, never loose in the caddy beside the bags. Coil the lead on its hook instead of leaving a loop hanging low, because a hanging loop at a toddler's height is a strangling risk.
Refill the bin when the level drops to the scoop, and keep one spare bag roll behind the one in use. Write the daily food amount on a label taped to the bin lid so whoever feeds gets the same answer.
When you clip the lead back on its hook after a walk, check the bag roll and swap it if it is down to the last few.

zones.purpose: Holds the small weather items the family grabs on the way out, for the season you are actually in.
zones.done: One open bin per person at their own height holding this season's gloves and hat with every pair matched, umbrellas standing points down in one stand by the door, and the other season's bin closed, labelled with the month you packed it, and up on the high shelf.

steps.text: Tip every glove, mitten and hat onto the floor and match them into pairs. Put the singles in one bag, and read the dates on the sun cream and the insect repellent, because a bottle opened two summers ago is no longer doing the job printed on the label.

Open bins with no lids, one per person, set at their own reach so a child can get their own gloves without asking anyone. Umbrellas go in the stand and never in a bin, because one wet umbrella soaks everything it lies against.

Everything goes into off-season storage washed and bone dry, because damp wool packed away in April comes out smelling in October. Wipe out the empty bins and get the sand out of the corners before you refill them.

Insect repellent and sun cream sitting in a low open bin will find their way into a small mouth, so anything carrying a warning on the label goes in a closed box above child reach. Store umbrellas points down, because a spike stood upright sits at a toddler's eye height.

Two changeovers a year, spring and autumn, and the month you closed a bin goes on its lid. Write the same short order on that lid as well: gloves matched, hats washed, creams checked for date, umbrellas emptied out.
The first cold morning you reach into the bin for gloves and find it empty is the signal, and the changeover happens that weekend.

zones.purpose: The tools that keep the entry floor and the door mats fit to walk on, kept where the mess actually lands.
zones.done: Broom, mop and dustpan clipped to the wall with their heads hanging clear of the floor, the vacuum parked flat against the wall inside a marked outline, and one caddy holding the four cleaners you genuinely use, each in its own labelled bottle.

steps.text: Line every bottle up on the floor and read them. Keep the floor cleaner, the glass spray, the disinfectant and the pet stain remover you actually reach for, and send out the last inch in the six other bottles, following the disposal line printed on each label.

Clip each long-handled tool near its head so the bristles hang clear of the floor and the handle points down. A broom stood on its bristles bends them out of shape and holds on to whatever it swept last.
Rinse the mop head and let it dry fully before it goes back on its clip, cut the hair off the vacuum's brush bar, and empty the dustpan rather than storing it loaded.

Never keep bleach and an ammonia-based cleaner in one closed caddy, because a leaking cap in a shut box mixes them into a gas you cannot get away from fast enough. This corner also holds a mains vacuum next to wet boots and a damp mop, so the socket and the flex stay up off the floor and dry.

The mop, broom and dustpan hang, and the vacuum parks inside its outline; nothing in this corner stands on the floor and nothing goes back on its clip wet. Paint or tape that outline so the empty space reads as a job done rather than a gap.
When you shake the door mats out, hang the broom back on its clip and feel whether the mop head has dried.

zones.purpose: Holds the sheets, towels, and blankets the beds in this house actually rotate through.
zones.done: Three sheet sets per bed, each nested inside one of its own pillowcases, with the bed size written on the shelf edge underneath. Everyday towels folded to one width in a stack no taller than your forearm. Two spare blankets on the top shelf with nothing balanced on them.

steps.text: Unfold every set and check it is complete and fits a bed you still own. The flat sheet whose fitted half vanished, fitted sheets with slack elastic that pop off a corner at three in the morning, and towels that smell sour an hour after drying all leave.
Fold each set to one uniform footprint and bundle it inside its own pillowcase so a bed change is one grab, not four. Queen and king low, everyday towels at chest height, guest blankets on top.

Pull every stack right out, wipe the shelf boards with a barely damp cloth, and let the wood dry fully before linens return. Watch for the grey line along the shelf lip that means dust is drifting down onto clean sheets.
A tall stack on a high shelf comes down as one mass when you tug the bottom towel. Keep no stack taller than your forearm, and keep the heavy blankets at waist height rather than overhead.
The shelf label carries the count, not just the name: "Queen, 3 sets." Anyone opening this door can see the shelf is short before laundry day rather than at bedtime.
Stripping a bed sends you here for the fresh bundle, and the count on the label tells you on the spot whether you are down to your last set.

zones.purpose: Parks the vacuum, broom, and mop so they come out in one motion and go back without a fight.
zones.done: The vacuum standing inside a taped floor outline with its cord wrapped and every crevice tool and brush head zipped in one bag clipped to its handle. Broom, mop, and duster hanging handle-down from wall clips with the heads clear of the floor. The closet door swinging fully open without touching anything.

steps.text: Stand every handle up and look at the working end. Brooms with splayed bristles that push dust rather than gather it, the mop head that no longer twists off its plate, and the old vacuum you keep for parts you have never once harvested all go out this week.

Fit a rail and hang each tool so bristles and mop heads swing free, because heads left standing on the floor bend over and re-soil what you just cleaned. Tape an outline for the vacuum's footprint and keep the attachments in one labeled bag clipped to its handle.

Empty the canister, cut the wound hair off the beater bar with scissors, rinse the mop head and dry it outside the closet. Sweep out the grit that drops off the vacuum wheels into the closet floor corners.
A broom leaned against the wall slides and lands across the doorway in the dark. Clip every handle to the rail, and never shut a damp mop head or a wet bucket into this closet.
The taped outline is the standard: if you can see floor inside the tape, the vacuum is out and not yet put away. The attachment bag rides on the handle, never loose on a shelf.
Switching the vacuum off is the signal to wrap the cord, not to lean it against the wall for later.

zones.purpose: Holds the products you clean with, grouped so you carry the right handful to the right room.
zones.done: Two or three caddies, each labeled on the end with the room it serves, every bottle wearing its original label, bleach products and ammonia products on separate shelves, and the whole zone up out of a small child's reach or behind a latch.

steps.text: Line every bottle up on the hallway floor. Anything decanted into an unmarked spray bottle gets disposed of according to its own instructions, and the specialty cleaner bought for one stain years ago goes with it. Only identical products get poured together.

Build a bathroom caddy and a kitchen caddy so you carry the whole job in one hand instead of walking back here twice. Gloves and cloths ride inside the caddy with the sprays, not in a drawer down the hall.
Wipe the crusted ring off the base of each bottle before it goes back, and lay a wipeable liner on the shelf so the next slow drip lands on plastic instead of soaking into the board.

Chlorine bleach and ammonia products release a choking gas if they leak onto each other, so give them separate shelves. Keep every product in its original labeled container, and put this zone out of a small child's reach or behind a latch.
Each caddy end reads the room it belongs to. The written rule is one line: a bottle without a legible original label is not stored, it is emptied.
Setting the caddy back on the shelf is when you notice what ran dry, and the empty goes on the shopping list before the door shuts.

zones.purpose: Keeps a reserve of paper goods, bulbs, and batteries so you never make a late-night emergency trip.
zones.done: Toilet roll in one clear bin with a card on the shelf edge reading "min 6, max 24". Bulbs in a labeled bin sorted by fitting. Batteries standing in their original packs in a shallow tray, sizes readable without lifting one out. Every bin label facing the door.

steps.text: Take the lot out. Loose batteries you cannot vouch for, bulbs for fittings you replaced when you went over to LED, and the bulk paper towel pack too big to lift down alone all leave now.

Toilet roll goes into the clear bin loose so you can see the level drop, bulbs stay in their boxes grouped by fitting, and batteries stand upright in a shallow tray by size so you read AAA from AA without picking one up. Heaviest packs at waist height, every label turned to the door.

Wipe the shelf and check the tray bottom for the white crust that means a cell has leaked. Press the underside of paper packs stored against a cold outside wall to feel for damp before you restock them.

Loose batteries whose terminals touch metal or each other can short and heat up, and a button cell dropped on a closet floor is exactly the size a toddler swallows. Keep cells in their packs, tape the terminals of any loose 9-volt, and store nothing at floor level here.
The minimum and maximum go on the shelf edge in front of each bin, not in your head. Below the minimum puts it on the shopping list; at the maximum you stop buying it regardless of the offer.
Lifting the last toilet roll out of the bin is the moment you are below the minimum, and it goes on the list before you leave the hallway.

zones.purpose: Parks the things you use a few weekends a year: guest bedding, decorations, and travel gear.
zones.done: Three or four lidded bins on the upper shelf, each labeled with what is inside and the month it was last closed. Guest pillows sealed in a zip bag. A shelf map taped inside the door showing which bin sits where, and nothing overhead heavy enough to need both hands.

steps.text: Every lid comes off, on the floor, in daylight. Decorations for a tree you no longer put up, the guest pillow gone flat and yellow, and the bin marked "misc" whose contents you cannot name without looking all go.
One bin per occasion, not one bin per overflow. Tape a shelf map inside the door so you can send someone else for the guest bedding without them unstacking the whole shelf to find it.

Guest bedding gets washed before it goes into the bin rather than after it comes out, because a year sealed in a box is what your guests will smell. Wipe the dust off each lid while it is open, and put your nose to the bottom of every bin for the mustiness that means something went in damp last season.

A heavy lidded bin lifted down from above your head is how ankles and backs go, especially when the lid blocks your view of your own feet. Keep the heaviest bins at chest height, and keep a proper step stool in this closet so nobody stands on a hallway chair.
Every bin carries its contents and the date it was last closed. Photograph each bin packed and tape the picture to the lid, so repacking has a target instead of a guess.
Taking the guest bed apart after a visit sends the bedding to the wash and then straight back into its own labeled bin, never onto the linen shelf.

zones.purpose: A small surface beside the stairs that holds a lamp and a landing spot, without becoming the house's holding pen for things headed to another floor.
zones.done: Three permanent things on the console top, say a lamp, a framed photo and one tray, with the tray holding nothing that was there yesterday. The lamp cord runs down the back leg in a clip, not across the walking side. One stair basket sits on the floor at the end nearest the top step, and it is empty.

steps.text: Take everything off the console top and out of its drawer in one sweep. Sort into three: things that genuinely live on this floor, things headed up or down (straight into the stair basket now), and the drift a landing collects, loose screws, dry pens, keys to nothing, mail you already read.

Put the tray at the end of the console nearest the top step, where your hand lands as you turn, not at the decorative centre. Clip the lamp cord to the back leg so it never crosses the side people walk.

Wipe the console top, the front edge where hips and bags push past, and the top rim of the lamp shade, which catches the dust the stairwell draught keeps lifting. Then press one corner of the console: if it rocks, shim it now, because a wobble beside an open stairwell is how a lamp goes over the edge.

Nothing on this surface may overhang the stair side, not by a centimetre. A book with its spine past the edge ends up on a tread, and a tread with a book on it is how people fall down stairs at night.

Write the count into the surface itself: three permanent items plus one tray on top, and one basket on the floor. Photograph the console in that state and tape the photo inside the console drawer, where the next person to open it will see it.
Whoever switches off the landing light at night carries the stair basket up or down and brings it back empty. The light switch is the trigger, so the basket never sleeps loaded.

zones.purpose: The frames, mirror and any sconces on the stairway wall, hung so they stay put and never crowd the shoulder of someone climbing with their arms full.
zones.done: Every frame level and hung from two points, each one the same vertical distance above the tread nose below it, so the gallery climbs on the stair's diagonal rather than fighting it. No sawtooth hanger and no single nail anywhere on the flight. Nothing projects more than a hand's width from the wall at shoulder height, and the mirror at the turn sits flat with no play when you push up on it.

steps.text: Take down anything hanging from a single nail or a sawtooth hanger, any frame with cracked glass, and the pictures you honestly last looked at years ago. You watch your feet on stairs, not the wall, so this wall only earns what you stop on the landing to look at.

Set the spacing by measuring from each frame's centre down to the nose of the tread beneath it and holding that number constant up the flight. Equal gaps between frames, and one consistent bottom edge across the flat landing section.

Dust the top edge of each frame first, then the glass, then wipe the wall along the turn where shoulders, bags and laundry baskets rub a grey line. As you take your hand off each frame, look behind it at the wire for kinks and at the hook for a bent lip.

Stair walls take constant vibration, and single nails and sawtooth hangers work loose in them. Everything here hangs from two points on hardware rated well above the item's weight, and the mirror goes into a stud or a proper wall anchor. Never straighten a high frame while standing on a tread. Do it from the flat landing or a properly footed ladder.

One hanging system across the whole wall, two hooks and a wire, so a replacement frame never quietly reintroduces a nail. Put a dated sticker on the back of the lowest frame recording the last time you press-tested the flight.

Handrail day is also frame day. As you work up the rail with your cloth, push up and out on the two frames within arm's reach. Over a season the whole wall gets checked without ever becoming a job you had to plan.

zones.purpose: The treads, runner, handrail and lighting that carry every person in the house between floors, several times a day, often with their arms full.
zones.done: Every tread bare from nose to riser, including the bottom three steps that usually stage things. The runner lies flat with no lifted corner at the turn. The handrail runs unbroken and unobstructed from the top newel post to the bottom, with no bag, coat or dog lead hung on either post. Both switches work, so the top step and the bottom step are lit before you take them.

steps.text: Nothing lives on stairs. Clear the folded laundry, the shoes, the box that has sat on step four since the weekend, all of it in one trip, and put each thing where it belongs on its own floor rather than restaging it on the landing above.

The one thing that must stay reachable here is the handrail, so strip both newel posts of coats, bags and leads. If a stair gate is fitted, set the top gate to swing away from the flight and never out over it.

Vacuum the tread noses, the crevice where each tread meets its riser, and along the stringer where a runner is tucked. That trapped grit is what polishes a runner slick under a stocking foot. Wipe the handrail its full length, including the underside your fingers wrap around.

Walk the flight slowly and test as you go: press each tread nose for movement, tug each runner edge, and grip the rail hard at top, middle and bottom to find a loose bracket. Then stand at the bottom in the dark and look at the top step, and stand at the top and look at the bottom. A burnt-out bulb over a top step is the single most dangerous thing in this room. Find it, and fix it now.

The standard is one sentence anyone in the house can check: bare treads, full width, lit at both ends, rail clear. Photograph the empty flight from the bottom and put that picture where the staging happens, which is almost always beside the bottom step.
The last person up at night takes the flight with one hand on the rail and carries whatever is sitting on a tread. If their hands are too full to hold the rail, that is the signal to make two trips.

zones.purpose: Seats people can drop into without checking them first, with the cushions kept dry.
zones.done: Four chairs you can sit in without testing, set close enough to talk across, every cushion in the deck box, and no cover crumpled on the ground behind a planter.

steps.text: Sit in every chair. The one that wobbles, the one with the cracked resin arm, and the cushion you would not offer a guest are decisions, not furniture. Count who actually sits out here on an ordinary evening and keep that many chairs plus two.

Chairs face each other close enough to talk without raising your voice, and no chair sits in the swing of the back door. Cushions live in the deck box, not stacked on a seat under a towel that stays wet underneath.

Hose the frames and scrub the webbing where grit packs into the joints, then stand each chair on its side so water runs out of the tubing instead of sitting inside it all summer. Check the underside of every cushion for black speckling while it dries.

Resin and plastic chairs go brittle from years of sun long before they look it. Flex each arm and press the seat pan hard with your palm; a chair that creaks or shows fine white cracks around a leg joint leaves today, not after someone drops through it onto the boards.

One cushion per seat and none spare, so a gap in the box tells you a cushion is still out on a chair. A photo of the chairs in their usual evening arrangement, taped inside the deck box lid, is what the last person out puts them back to.
When you carry the last glass inside for the night, the cushions come in with you in the same trip.

zones.purpose: Cook over fire without leaving the grill to find a tool or wondering if there is gas.
zones.done: Grates scraped bare, grease tray emptied and back in its rails, four tools on the grill's own hooks and no fifth anywhere, the propane tank upright with its level written on the collar, and a clear arm's length between the grill body and the siding, railing, and umbrella canopy.

steps.text: Empty the side shelf and the cabinet under the grill. Out comes a bag of dried-out lighter cubes, three sets of tongs, a thermometer with a dead battery, and sauce bottles that spent a whole summer at outdoor temperature. Keep one long-handled tong, one spatula, one instant-read thermometer, and one basting brush.

Hang the tongs and spatula on the grill's own hooks so you never walk away from a lit grill to go looking. Fuel keeps its distance from heat: the propane tank upright and outdoors, the charcoal bag sealed and off the ground, the chimney starter beside it.

Burn the grates off, then pull the flavorizer bars and scrape the grease tray and drip pan out into the bin rather than leaving a rendered layer to feed the next flare-up. While the burners are exposed, look up into the tubes; a spider web in a venturi tube is exactly why the flame runs yellow and lazy along one side.

Brush soapy water onto the propane hose and the regulator fitting, then open the valve. Bubbles mean replace the hose, not tighten it and hope. Retire any wire brush whose bristles you can pull free with your fingers, because a loose bristle ends up in food, and switch to a scraper or a coiled brush.

The grease tray gets emptied on a fixed count of cooks, marked off on a card taped inside the cabinet door. A tank is written full or empty in marker on its collar the same day it changes state, so nobody has to guess by lifting it.
Every time you close the lid at the end of a cook, scrape the grates while they are still hot and glance into the tray before you walk away.

zones.purpose: Feed people outdoors without carrying the kitchen out in four trips.
zones.done: A bare tabletop except the umbrella and one weighted tray, six chairs tucked fully under, string lights clipped along the rail with no cord crossing the floor, and nothing stored beneath the table.

steps.text: Clear the table down to bare surface and face what has been living on it: a citronella bucket burned to the rim, a lighter that no longer sparks, placemats gone pale on the upper side only, and the melamine plates from a barbecue two summers ago. Settle the dishware question below before anything goes back.

Chairs tuck fully under the table so nobody has to sidestep a chair leg carrying a hot dish. One weighted tray holds the salt, the pepper, and the napkin weight, so laying the table is one trip out rather than four.

Wash the tabletop along the grain and pay attention to the collar where the umbrella pole passes through, since that ring collects grit and holds water against the table. Wipe the underside edges too, which is where hands go and where wasps like to start building.

An open umbrella is a sail. Match the base weight to the canopy size, crank the umbrella down whenever you leave the table, and close it before wind arrives rather than during it. Run string lights on hooks along the rail using outdoor-rated cord on a socket with a residual current device, never a household extension lead lying across boards that get wet.
The table's resting state is bare except for the umbrella and the one weighted tray. Anything else arrives with a meal and leaves with it, including the candles.
The last person carrying a plate inside closes the umbrella and lifts the tray on the way past.

zones.purpose: Keep the containers alive and keep everything that feeds them off the ground and out of reach.
zones.done: Every saucer empty, pots nested by size along the wall with drain holes clear, one tool caddy holding trowel, pruners, and gloves, and a latched chemical box above the tools with no more in it than you can name from the doorway.

steps.text: Turn out every empty pot. A pot with no drainage hole and a pot still holding last year's dead root ball both go; keep the pots you will actually plant this season plus two, nested by size. Bagged potting soil that has gone solid and sour gets emptied into a bed rather than stored for a spring that will not want it.

Hand tools stand in one caddy you can carry in the hand that is not holding the watering can. Long tools hang head up on a rail so no blade waits at shin height. Fertilizer and every concentrate sit above the tools, never in the row beside the watering can where a tired hand reaches.

Empty every saucer, then scrub the white mineral crust from the pot rims and scrape soil off the trowel and pruner blades before they go back damp. Wipe the pruner blades and put a drop of oil on the pivot while you have them open.

The concentrates, slug pellets, and fertilizer are the real hazard on this patio, and pellets look like food to a dog. They stay in a latched box, up high, in the container they came in, never decanted into a drink bottle or a jam jar. Empty standing water from saucers, the wheelbarrow, and the upturned pot lid after rain so mosquitoes have nowhere to breed.
Every pot carries a small tag with what is in it and the month it went in, so anyone in the house can decide whether it needs water without coming to find you.
When you fill the watering can, look along the row of saucers before you start pouring.

zones.purpose: Get the cushions under a lid within a minute of the first drop of rain.
zones.done: The lid closes flat without anyone pressing down, cushions in one layer on top, two labelled totes beneath them, and the floor of the box visible the moment the cushions come out.

steps.text: Empty the deck box onto the boards, all of it. You will find cushions that went in damp last autumn, a croquet set missing two mallets, four covers for furniture you no longer own, and a bag of charcoal that has drawn moisture and will never light properly again. Anything that still smells of mildew after a wash does not go back in.

Cushions load last and come out first, because they are the only thing in this box that has to move in a hurry. Games and covers go into flat-bottomed totes underneath, so nothing loose migrates into the corners where hands do not reach.

Scrub the interior and prop the lid open on a dry, breezy day until the corners are genuinely dry rather than just cool to the touch. Check that the drain holes in the base are clear, and tip the box forward to sweep out the layer of leaf mulch that has packed underneath it.

A deck box lid is heavy and hinged at exactly a child's hand height. Lift it and let go halfway; if it drops on its own, fit a lid stay before anything else, because crushed fingers in that hinge is the injury this zone reliably produces. Mouse droppings or shredded nesting material in stored fabric means you wash before folding, wearing gloves, and check the box for the gap they came in through.

Two totes, one written games and one written covers, labelled on the short end you can read once the cushions are lifted out. The lid is the measure: if someone has to sit on it to close it, something leaves the box that day.
When the cushions go in at the end of an evening, the lid gets latched, not just lowered.

zones.purpose: The structure you stand on and lean against, kept sound and kept clear.
zones.done: Nothing on the deck that is not furniture, daylight visible through the gaps between boards, no green film on the shaded treads, and every rail post immovable when you push it hard.

steps.text: This zone earns its state by having nothing stored in it. The planter that has drifted into the walking route, the hose coiled across the top step, and the bag of paving sand leaning on a rail post all come off the deck entirely, because each of them holds damp against the wood it sits on as well as standing in your way.

Walk the route from the door to the steps to the gate carrying a full laundry basket in both arms so you cannot see your feet. Whatever you have to step around gets moved. The mat sits square at the threshold with its edges lying flat, not curling up at a corner.

Rake the gaps between boards clear with a putty knife or a paint stirrer, because a blocked gap holds water against the board ends and that is precisely where rot begins. Then scrub the green algae film off the shaded boards and the stair treads, which is the slipperiest surface anywhere on the property after rain.

Grab the top rail at every post and push hard, outward and then down. Any movement, any softness under your thumb, any screw head standing proud is a stop and fix today. Check that every stair tread rises the same height as the ones above and below it, and that the step lights still come on, because one odd riser in the dark is how people go down. Find it, and fix it now.

A dated tag inside the back door records when the rail was last pushed and the boards last probed, so the next check starts from a written date rather than an argument about whether you did it in spring.
Every time you sweep the deck, push the rail at two posts before the broom goes away.
